items.blurb: Acute kidney injury (AKI) is a common clinical problem with high morbidity and mortality due to frequently occurring secondary organ complications, including acute neurologic dysfunction, such as delirium. Specific mechanisms responsible for this kidney-brain crosstalk are unknown but hypothesized to include uremic toxins and neuroinflammation secondary to systemic inflammation. Here we show that uremic mice with AKI show hippocampal monocytic neuroinflammation associated with acute delirium-like neurologic dysfunction only in the presence of circulating osteopontin fragments. Mechanistically, circulating osteopontin (OPN/Spp1) released by the injured kidney was cleaved by thrombin in the lung into OPN-N and OPN-C-terminal fragments. Both OPN fragments were required to drive upregulation of the monocyte chemoattractant chemokine-ligand-2 (CCL2) in hippocampal endothelial cells. AKI mice lacking OPN or unable to activate OPN by thrombin cleavage showed kidney injury and serum uremic toxin elevations like wt controls but were protected from hippocampal CCL2 upregulation, monocyte recruitment, and delirium-like symptoms. Systemic application of an OPN or CCL2 neutralizing antibody was protective. Our results suggest that a specific kidney-released circulating factor, osteopontin, drives acute neurologic dysfunction after AKI and challenge the widely held hypothesis that uremic toxins play a dominant role. They also identify thrombin cleavage of OPN as a potential therapeutic target and critical switch for the remote functions of circulating OPN.

items.title: Aging remodels the neuronal activity-dependent transcriptome
items.blurb: Experience-driven neuronal activity induces coordinated transcriptional programs in neurons and glia that support plasticity and memory. How aging reshapes these activity-regulated gene (ARG) programs, and whether activity mitigates or exacerbates aging phenotypes, remain open questions with implications for cognitive decline. Here, we develop novel-environment and chemogenetic paradigms to characterize age-dependent remodeling of ARG transcriptomes in the mouse hippocampus at single-cell resolution. Aging contracts youthful ARG programs in both gene number and dynamic range, a contraction that persists under controlled chemogenetic stimulation independent of behavior. In parallel, novel experience in older mice reveals a latent transcriptional competence. First, distinct sets of genes respond to neuronal activity selectively in older cells. Second, enhancing activity in older animals partially reverses, or buffers, basal aging-associated changes across the transcriptome. Novel experience counteracts aging-associated changes in the target genes of the memory regulator CREB1 and the ER-stress sensor ATF6 across cell types. These data constitute a resource for neuronal activity-dependent transcription across the lifespan and identify a basis for the benefits of cognitive engagement: novel experience buffers age-related transcriptional drift.

items.title: Counterfactual aging in individual digital twin brains uncovers a latent dimension of resilience to aging
items.blurb: Cognitive reserve concerns why the same aging causes less decline in some individuals than others, a question that digital twin brains can address by aging each individual in silico. Here we present Brain-VRNN, a connectome-constrained variational recurrent neural network trained on longitudinal multitask functional MRI. Its regenerated brain signals reproduced four functional aging markers of unseen individuals (r = 0.93-0.96) and identified each person (accuracy 0.98). Without cognitive scores, its global latent learned a trait dimension stable within each person, which helped predict future cognition. Crucially, when every individual underwent the same counterfactual aging, those with a lower trait value declined more, yet recovered up to 1.6 times as much with a reduction in body mass index, a modifiable dementia risk factor. Aging single regions showed that different markers decline through different regions, with a lateral temporal-angular region shared by all. Brain-VRNN brings within-person simulation to cognitive reserve.

items.title: PROGMF: Progressive Multimodal Fusion and Representation Learning for Incomplete Neuroimaging Data
items.blurb: Multimodal neuroimaging studies often involve cohorts with partially overlapping data modalities. Many conventional multimodal fusion methods rely on participants with complete observations across the selected modalities. We introduce Progressive Multimodal Fusion (ProgMF), a novel fusion framework for learning multimodal source representations from incomplete neuroimaging data without imputing missing observations. ProgMF integrates modalities sequentially through independent vector analysis (IVA), cross-stage component alignment, and anchor-guided representation transfer, allowing information learned from earlier-stage cohorts to inform subsequent multimodal decompositions. We evaluated ProgMF on four neuroimaging-inspired synthetic modalities, while varying subject overlap, observation noise, modality relatedness, and fusion orders. ProgMF generally achieved lower source-recovery errors than complete-case IVA and the evaluated imputation-based methods, with larger improvements as multimodal subject overlap decreased. We further applied ProgMF to structural MRI gray matter, resting-state functional network connectivity, and 18F-florbetapir (AV45) amyloid positron emission tomography data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. ProgMF achieved higher mean cross-modal fusion scores than the imputation-based baselines and a modest improvement over complete-case IVA. Among the 293 participants with complete multimodal observations, two recovered source component vectors showed significant associations with clinical diagnosis across cognitively normal, mild cognitive impairment, and dementia groups. Both sources were also significantly associated with cognitive performance and dementia severity. The recovered sources exhibited diagnosis-related structural and amyloid PET patterns involving regions such as the hippocampi, precuneus, and cingulate cortices. Our findings support progressive representation transfer as an effective approach for recovering coherent, interpretable multimodal sources from participants with incomplete modality coverage.

items.title: Precision of sensory representations in cortex is indexed by alpha power and pupil dilation, and tracks the dynamics of correlated noise
items.blurb: Sensory representations fluctuate in precision from moment to moment, shaping the fidelity of perception and memory. Population-coding theory proposes that these fluctuations are constrained by correlated variability within neural populations, yet linking these mechanisms to behaviour and brain state in humans has remained challenging. Here we combined EEG with an encoding-decoding framework to reconstruct orientation-selective population responses and quantify representational precision dynamically over time. Precision predicted subsequent working-memory performance and evolved in close correspondence with the dynamics of correlated variability between decoded orientation channels. Following stimulus onset, correlated variability was selectively suppressed among similarly tuned channels, the pattern predicted to maximise coding fidelity. Prestimulus alpha power and pupil size independently predicted representational precision, linking these dynamics to endogenous cortical and neuromodulatory state. Together, these findings identify candidate mechanisms and accessible physiological markers of representational precision in humans.

items.title: Commentary on the nomenclatural status of Benthoctopus Grimpe, 1921 (Cephalopoda: Octopoda) and redescription of "Vulcanoctopus" pseudonymus (Grimpe, 1922)
items.blurb: The nomenclatural status of the two octopus genera Bathypolypus Grimpe, 1921 and Benthoctopus Grimpe, 1921 has been the subject of considerable, at times contentious debate since both genera were first proposed. Of the two, Bathypolypus has nomenclatural priority, being the first mentioned of the two in Grimpe's cursory note. Although Benthoctopus was relegated to synonymy of Bathypolypus in 2002, the case for this synonymy was not compelling. The systematic complications generated by this act were subsequently aggravated by the description of another taxon, Muusoctopus Gleadall, 2004 (a replacement name proposed for taxa formerly attributed to Benthoctopus) and molecular data, that subsequently demonstrated Muusoctopus to be a junior synonym of Vulcanoctopus Gonzalez & Guerra, 1998. This created an untenable situation where multiple competing names were available to apply to many generally deep-dwelling octopus species with two rows of suckers, no ink sac, and either smooth or papillose bodies. Remnants of one important specimen historically attributed to the type species of the genus Benthoctopus (Be. piscatorum (Verrill, 1879)) are herein redescribed. Historical descriptions of this specimen are combined with modern observations and critically compared with what is reported for other North Atlantic Bathypolypus and Vulcanoctopus taxa to critique the original synonymy of Benthoctopus with Bathypolypus. The analysis demonstrates that the original synonymy of Benthoctopus with Bathypolypus cannot be upheld based on existing data, and the widespread nomenclatural repercussions of this status change are discussed. Finally, the type and only known specimen of Vulcanoctopus pseudonymus (Grimpe, 1922) comb. nov. is partly redescribed to facilitate a broader-scale revision of these problematic North Atlantic octopuses.

items.title: Solanaceae-derived spirostane saponins inhibit dengue virus replication and remodel host-cell metabolism
items.blurb: Flaviviruses reprogram host-cell metabolism to support viral replication. In previous work, we showed that Solanaceae-derived spirostane saponins inhibit dengue virus replication and were predicted to interact with viral enzymes. Here, we investigated whether S01, a purified solid from Solanum ovalifolium containing predominantly two characterized spirostane saponins, also modulates host-cell metabolism in association with reduced permissiveness to dengue virus serotype 2 (DENV-2). We performed untargeted GC-QTOF-MS metabolomics in Vero cells under four conditions, including untreated control, S01 treatment, DENV-2 infection, and DENV-2 infection with S01 treatment. Quality-control samples clustered tightly, supporting analytical reproducibility. Principal component analysis revealed separation among experimental groups, and PERMANOVA confirmed significant global metabolic differences (F = 27.567, R{superscript 2} = 0.827, p = 0.001). S01 also retained strong antiviral activity, producing 99.9% inhibition under the metabolomics conditions. DENV-2 infection was associated with alterations metabolites related to amino acid, carbohydrate, lipid, and sphingolipid metabolism. Pathway analysis highlighted glutamate metabolism, arginine and proline metabolism, glycolysis-related pathways, fatty-acid oxidation and carnitine-associated metabolism, phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis, and sphingolipid metabolism. In uninfected cells, S01 induced a distinct metabolic profile (OPLS-DA R{superscript 2}Y = 0.951, Q{superscript 2} = 0.851; permutation p = 0.002), characterized by increased carbohydrate-related metabolites, including the unresolved Talose/D-glucose feature, gluconic acid, 2-keto-L-gulonic acid, and D-mannitol, together with decreased abundance of selected lipid-related metabolites. During infection, S01 induced a distinct metabolic (OPLS-DA R{superscript 2}Y = 0.928, Q{superscript 2} = 0.841), characterized by lower abundance of several fatty-acid-related and organic-acid metabolites and higher abundance of carbohydrate-related metabolites, while modifying selected DENV-2-associated metabolic alterations. These findings associate S01 antiviral activity with substantial remodeling of host-cell metabolism. Together with previous docking predictions of interactions with viral targets, the results support a model in which the antiviral activity of Solanaceae-derived spirostane saponins may involve complementary effects on viral and host-associated processes.

items.title: ATSASfold: a web server integrating AlphaFold models with ATSAS-based SAXS analysis
items.blurb: Small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) is routinely used for the structural characterization of protein monomers in solution, and computational prediction methods such as AlphaFold now provide accurate atomic models for most proteins. When a predicted model and the experimental scattering curve disagree, several refinement strategies exist, but selecting the appropriate one remains difficult, particularly for users without SAXS modeling expertise. ATSASfold is a web server developed to help analyse the results of SAXS measurements on protein monomers and select appropriate refinement strategies. From a provided experimental SAXS curve, ATSASfold performs primary data analysis, gives a general assessment of macromolecules shape, size, possible aggregation state and data quality. An AlphaFold-generated model is fitted against the SAXS curve and the agreement with the experiment is evaluated. In cases where the fit shows significant discrepancies, a machine-learning classifier trained on SASBDB depositions assigns the case to one of four categories, suggesting the most relevant ATSAS-based strategy for model refinement: fixed model fitting, rigid-body modelling, normal-mode analysis or ensemble optimization. When needed, a graphical interface allows the user to adjust domains or flexible regions of the protein before submitting the structure to ATSAS online for longer fitting jobs. After the fitting is completed, ATSASfold provides a summary of the results. The workflow was tested on examples from the SASBDB open web-databank. These use cases demonstrate smooth operation of the web server and show how ATSASfold can simplify the transition from SAXS data collection to structure-based interpretation.

items.title: Integrating disease and protein networks expands genetic support for therapeutic targets
items.blurb: Human genetics guides therapeutic target selection, but direct genetic support covers few clinically investigated target-indication pairs, each linking a target to a disease. Here we introduce BRIDGE (Biological Relation-Informed Diffusion of Genetic Evidence), which propagates genetic evidence through coupled protein-protein interaction and disease-similarity networks. Each candidate's score is calibrated against scores obtained after randomly substituting similarly connected genes for genes with direct genetic support. In a retrospective benchmark of 13,022 pairs that had reached at least phase I, BRIDGE supported 572 additional pairs, increasing coverage from 5.1% to 9.5%. Among eligible pairs lacking direct genetic support, 25.3% of network-added pairs had reached launch versus 8.6% of remaining candidates (relative success, 2.94; 95% confidence interval, 2.51-3.45). This enrichment extended to 158 pairs involving 101 genes with no direct genetic support in the benchmark. At a matched selection size of 1,310 pairs, BRIDGE ranking captured 265 launched pairs, compared with 223 under a rule transferring support across neighbouring targets or indications. These findings show that coupling disease relationships with protein connectivity expands the reach of human genetics to additional therapeutic targets and indications while retaining clinical relevance.

items.title: GenVinci reconstructs 3D molecular tissue scenes from histology to map senescence across aging and disease
items.blurb: Spatial omics has generated measurements at unprecedented scale, yet computational approaches remain largely confined to individual modalities and 2D representations. Here we assemble ImageOmicsNet-300M, a corpus of 300 million single-cell and spatial transcriptomic profiles, including 24.9 million H&E-predicted virtual spatial transcriptomics profiles, and 4,623 H&E sections. Of these H&E sections, we generated 1,782 from aging mouse organs and serially sectioned human skin spanning five decades, with matched spatial transcriptomics and snRNA-seq. Building on this resource, we develop GenVinci, a multimodal tissue foundation model that reconstructs 3D tissue scenes from routine 2D histology. GenVinci predicts spatial gene expression from H&E with zero-shot generalization and maps senescence-associated states across 85.8 million cells, revealing cell-type-specific patterns and disease-associated remodeling. Integration with human genetics implicates suprabasal keratinocytes in atopic dermatitis and keratinocyte carcinomas, linked to higher and lower p16 and p21 expression, respectively. These findings establish GenVinci as a framework mapping senescence in 3D across scales.

items.title: Benchmarking four large language models on generating and selecting hypotheses that match published findings in 50 studies of ageing biology
items.blurb: Objective We asked how often hypotheses generated by large language models for 50 research tasks matched the withheld finding of the published study, and whether model forecasts could identify the matching hypotheses. Methods We built tasks from 50 peer-reviewed studies in ageing biology published after the models' stated training cutoffs; each task gave the background and a research question and withheld the study's finding (the reference finding). GPT-6 Astra, Grok 4.5, Claude Opus 5.5, and Gemini 4 Argon each generated five hypotheses per task by three methods: a single request, a multistep pipeline, and the Omega Point method without literature search (2997 hypotheses). A hypothesis matched the reference finding if at least two of three judge models from other developers scored it at least 3 (primary threshold) or at least 4 (strict threshold) on a 0 to 5 scale; refusals counted as non-matches. A selection rule, chosen from 112 variants evaluated on the Grok 4.5 hypotheses, kept only the hypotheses for which all four predictor models forecast experimental confirmation; the predictors never saw the published finding. The controls were recorded random answers and each generator's first-listed hypothesis. Confidence intervals (95% CIs) were calculated by cluster bootstrap over tasks. Results Of the hypotheses generated by a single request, 13.2% to 18.0% matched the reference finding, compared with 11.2% to 18.8% for the multistep pipeline and 2.8% to 7.6% for the Omega Point method. With a single request, the hypothesis listed first matched in 37.5% of cases (75/200), and the hypotheses in positions 2 to 5 matched in 10.1% (81/800). Among the hypotheses selected unanimously, the match rate was 73.7% (14/19) for Grok 4.5, 47.4% (9/19) for Gemini 4 Argon, and 63.6% (14/22) for Claude Opus 5.5, compared with 12.1% to 17.9% for the random control and 37.5% to 40.0% for the first-listed hypotheses. The selected lists captured 27.3% to 35.0% of all matching hypotheses. Pooled across the three sets, the match rate among selected hypotheses exceeded that among first-listed hypotheses by 23.2 percentage points (pp; 95% CI [13.0, 32.6]). When Gemini 4 Argon re-extracted the reference findings, the match rate among selected hypotheses was 59.6% (34/57), compared with 61.4% (35/57) against the original reference findings for the same tasks. In a manual audit with the generator, judge scores, and selection status hidden, our classifications agreed with the judges' at the primary threshold in 81/100 cases (Cohen's kappa 0.62). Agreement was 89.7% after weighting the sample strata by their size in the corpus. We classified 19 of 30 sampled selected hypotheses as matches, and the judges classified 20 of 30. Conclusions In the evaluated sets, unanimous selection by the four predictors increased the match rate among selected hypotheses; the resulting match rate depended on the matching threshold. Generators listed a matching hypothesis first more often than in later positions, and 50 of the 60 selected hypotheses were listed first. The advantage over the first-listed hypotheses and over the best single predictor at equal list length was statistically significant for the Grok and Opus hypotheses but not for the Gemini hypotheses, and the pairwise differences of the advantage between generators were not statistically significant (p >= 0.16 after Holm correction). We selected the rule using the Grok hypotheses and evaluated it on the Gemini and Opus hypotheses for the same 50 tasks; it has not been tested on new tasks.

items.title: Learning spatial cellular state through 3D reconstruction of the cell
items.blurb: Subcellular-resolution spatial transcriptomics localizes individual RNA transcripts within cells with high-precision. Existing methods for identifying spatially organized cell populations rely on cellular niches defined by neighboring cells, leaving open whether such populations can be identified from individual-cell representations alone. Moreover, representations that jointly capture transcript identity and three-dimensional (3D) spatial organization have not been systematically learned or biologically evaluated. Here we present a representation learning framework that models each cell as a gene-annotated point cloud of transcripts and trains a rotation-equivariant neural network to reconstruct 3D cell shape, yielding spatially informed transcript embeddings. We further aggregate these embeddings into a cell-state representation that summarizes transcript-level spatial patterns. Our framework outperforms existing point-cloud-based 3D reconstruction methods on cell-shape reconstruction. In MERFISH human uterine cancer, combining the learned embeddings with gene expression improved prediction of CD45RO protein intensity over both gene expression alone and niche-based embeddings. Applied to MERFISH human liver cancer and Xenium human lung datasets, our framework identified distinct spatial patterns between cell populations, including spatially organized subpopulations marked by disease-associated gene expression and patterns associated with pathological tissue structures. Together, these results show that learning transcript representations through 3D cell reconstruction provides a novel approach to capture cell-state heterogeneity and biologically relevant spatial organization in subcellular spatial transcriptomics.

items.title: Quantifying Homology and Length Bias in Antimicrobial Peptide Prediction
items.blurb: Bacteria are becoming resistant to existing antibiotics faster than new ones are found. Antimicrobial peptides are a promising alternative, but laboratory testing is slow and costly. Candidates are therefore ranked first by a classifier, and published classifiers report near-perfect accuracy. Two controls are missing from the benchmarks behind those numbers. Training and test peptides are not separated by sequence homology. The negative class is not matched to the positive class by length. We propose a controlled evaluation protocol that imposes both, plus a sample-size control that separates matching from the data it removes. We apply it to a four-model ensemble of our own and ten baselines on a benchmark of 16,168 sequences, holding the models fixed. A classifier given nothing but peptide length separates the benchmark far above chance. Homology control costs 0.067 MCC and length matching a further 0.115, taking the reported score from 0.834 to 0.661. Over ten redrawn partitions the length term holds while the homology term shrinks, so length is the effect that survives. The protocol also reorders the methods, and a frozen ESM-2 embedding overtakes the ensemble. Three published benchmarks show the same pattern. We recommend a minimum reporting standard that makes such losses visible.

items.title: spicyR enables robust, well-powered co-localisation tests in large spatial omics cohorts
items.blurb: Spatial omics technologies can now profile finely resolved cell populations in patient tissue at scale, offering a way to link their arrangement to outcomes. Yet images often differ in size, shape and cell content, and existing tests between patient groups mistake these differences for co-localisation or weight every image equally. We present spicyR v2, which avoids both problems with a fast, permutation-free test that accounts for these differences and weights each image by how precisely it measures co-localisation. In simulations and 74 analyses of 42 public datasets, it controlled false discoveries, had more power than spicyR v1 and was robust to tears, holes and differences in cell number that misled other methods. These analyses also revealed that many studies relating co-localisation to clinical outcomes are underpowered, and spicyR v2 can estimate the number of patients a new study needs. spicyR v2 analyses 100 million cells in minutes, making robust, well-powered tests of co-localisation practical for large spatial omics cohorts.

items.title: LipidRT: leveraging retention time coherence for robust lipid annotation in reversed-phase LC-MS-based lipidomics
items.blurb: MS/MS data alone is often insufficient for confident lipid identification, while existing retention time (RT)-based methods, despite their promise, have limited applicability. We present LipidRT, an R-based Shiny application that uses RT coherence to validate, refine and expand lipid annotations in untargeted RPLC-HRMS lipidomics in a dataset-specific, software-agnostic manner. By exploiting conserved chromatographic elution relationships as structural constraints and excluding RT-inconsistent annotations from model fitting, LipidRT improves annotation confidence, coverage and consistency while minimizing manual curation.

items.title: MARRI: Mechanism-Aware Learning of RNA-RNA Interactions with Foundation Models
items.blurb: RNA-RNA interactions (RRIs) are central to post-transcriptional regulation, yet their prediction requires accounting for structural accessibility and intermolecular base pairing beyond sequence complementarity. Pretrained RNA foundation models provide representations of individual RNAs, but translating these representations into interaction predictions requires mechanistic knowledge of interaction recognition. Here, we introduce MARRI, a mechanism-aware multimodal framework that couples pretrained representations with domain knowledge by embedding learned opening penalties and hybridization gains into bidirectional cross-RNA attention. MARRI improves ROC--AUC and PR--AUC over the strongest baseline by 12.20% and 10.25%, respectively, and maintains strong discrimination for unseen RNA partnerships and interaction regions. Perturbation and repeat-context analyses identify prediction-relevant sequence regions. Integrating MARRI-derived interaction propensities with disease-associated expression profiles links molecular prediction to systems-level models of disease progression and network remodeling. MARRI thus illustrates a knowledge-guided strategy for coupling molecular foundation models with domain knowledge to support grounded prediction, interpretation and systems-level hypothesis generation.

items.title: Comparative metagenomics reveals diversity and metabolic heterogeneity of sediment microbes from the Great Barrier Reef
items.blurb: Microbial communities in coral reefs are highly connected through benthic-pelagic coupling. Pelagic and host-associated microbiomes have recently been characterised via genome-resolved metagenomics. However, similar characterisation of sediment communities has lagged behind due to their higher complexity. Here, using short- and long-read shotgun sequence data, we characterised sediment microbial communities of Australia's Great Barrier Reef. From 191 samples across 48 broadly distributed sites, we recovered 2,698 prokaryotic metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) representing 1,201 species-level clusters, most of which are novel. Compared against their sympatric counterparts in seawater, sediment MAGs exhibited greater phylogenetic diversity and flexibility in metabolic potential, implicating diverse respiration strategies and cycling of nitrogen, sulphur, and hydrogen. They also encode more abundant and novel biosynthetic capabilities, likely reflecting competition and adaptation to intermittent fluctuations in nutrient regimes, and between oxic and anoxic conditions. Our results provide foundational genomic resources for reef sediment microbes, uncovering biodiversity and function that together with planktonic microbes shape the ecological success and stability of coral reef ecosystems.

items.title: Multimodal Structural and Regulatory Architecture of Coding and Non-Coding Variants Across the Orofacial Clefting TP63-IRF6-GRHL3 Network
items.blurb: Pathogenic variation across the TP63-IRF6-GRHL3 transcriptional network causes syndromic and nonsyndromic orofacial clefts (OFCs), yet scalar sequence predictors collapse distinct failure modes and leave isoform-specific coding variants, splice-altering indels, and distal enhancer alleles unresolved. Here, we integrate 29 AlphaFold 3 (AF3) assemblies (10 wild-type, 19 mutant), thermodynamic stability ({Delta}{Delta}G) calculations, and AlphaGenome regulatory modeling across clinical, saturation-mutagenesis, and reporter benchmarks. In strict leave-one-gene-out (LOGO) coding benchmarks, replacing paralog crystal templates with full-length human AF3 structures improves IRF6 classification (biophysical AUROC rising from 0.7844 to 0.8967; {Delta}{Delta}G from 0.6461 to 0.8516) and resolves canonical isoform gaps in the 602-residue MANE Select GRHL3 homodimer. Projecting IRF6 missense variants onto a two-dimensional stability-versus-interface phase plane separates dominant-negative popliteal pterygium syndrome (PPS) poisons from haploinsufficient Van der Woude syndrome (VWS1) alleles (VWS1-versus-PPS Quadrant I odds ratio [OR] = 0.0263 [reciprocal OR = 38.0], p = 4.652 x 10-3) and distinguishes DNA-contact poisons from dimer-unfolding alleles across 12 zebrafish in vivo assays. Atomistic base-readout contacts in the AF3 TP63-MCS9.7 tetramer mirror loss-of-function profiles in MaveDB ({rho} = 0.6048, p = 6.52 x 10-4) and AlphaGenome keratinocyte DNase predictions ({rho} = 0.6040, p = 6.65 x 10-4). Across non-coding benchmarks, AlphaGenome splicing tracks reach an AUROC of 0.9876 while prioritizing cryptic splice variants of uncertain significance, and epithelial chromatin tracks capture enhancer grammar, plasmid-cloning artifacts, and context-dependent ARHGAP29, FOXE1, and local 8q24 chromatin effects within AlphaGenome's 1.049-Mb horizon.

items.title: Systematic prediction of genetic variance in a line development program
items.blurb: To date, predicting the genetic variance (VG) in biparental crosses has been unreliable. My objective was to determine if predicting VG via tabular analysis, which was developed assuming free recombination and having known VG in founder crosses, is effective even if these unrealistic assumptions are unmet. With line X being developed from the P1/P2 cross, the VG in X/Y was predicted as VX/Y = {lambda}1VP1/Y + {lambda}2VP2/Y, where {lambda}1 was the parental contribution of P1 to X and {lambda}2 was the parental contribution of P2 to X. Simulations involved four founder lines with biallelic marker loci and multiple alleles at quantitative trait loci. The VG in each founder cross was estimated from simulated phenotypic values of N lines under varying heritability (h2). Non-founder lines were developed successively from the founders. Among the 774 non-founder crosses, the mean correlation between the true VG and predicted VG ranged from 0.49 (N = 50 and h2 = 0.20) to 0.70 (N = 400 to 1000 and h2 [≥] 0.50). The mean regression of predicted VG on true VG was 0.51-0.52. Having N = 100-200 lines was sufficient for estimating VG. Free recombination increased the regression of predicted VG on true VG to 0.87 and the correlation between the two to 0.64-0.93. Overall, the results suggested that tabular analysis is currently the most effective method for predicting VG. Further research is needed on combining VG estimates in both founder and non-founder crosses when conducting tabular analysis in a breeding program.

items.title: The evolution of sexual dimorphism in the weapon system of leaf-footed bugs (Hemiptera: Coreoidea)
items.blurb: The natural world contains an extraordinary diversity of morphologically elaborate traits, yet the evolutionary processes underlying the emergence and diversification of sexual dimorphism in these structures are not fully resolved. Some of the most extravagant of these traits are the mechanical weapons of sexual selection. They include such noteworthy structures as the tusks of narwals and the mandibles of stag beetles. Such traits are notoriously sexually dimorphic -- often elaborated in one sex while absent or reduced in the other sex. The mechanisms by which sexual dimorphism evolves in such traits is only just beginning to be understood. Existing macroevolutionary studies have examined simple structures or have simplified elaborate and complex weapons using binary coding or metrics, limiting the insights that can be gained. Here, we investigated the macroevolutionary dynamics of sexual dimorphism across 14 traits in bodies and complex, elaborate weaponry of leaf-footed bugs (Hemiptera: Coreoidea) using phylogenomic data and quantitative and qualitative trait analyses. Phylogenetic generalized linear mixed models across 27 species showed that females are generally larger-bodied, whereas males exhibit greater exaggeration in most putative weapon traits, often with steeper allometric scaling. Ancestral state estimation across 154 species revealed that sexual dimorphism is evolutionarily labile and heterogeneous across traits. Contrary to expectations from classical models, sexual dimorphism most commonly arose when new traits originated in both sexes already in a dimorphic state, rather than through subsequent divergence from ancestrally shared, monomorphic traits or as a sex-limited trait. At the level of entire weapon system, sexual dimorphism varied widely across lineages, clustered phylogenetically, and reached extreme levels through coordinated changes across multiple traits. By showing that complex weapon systems diversify through semi-independent changes and that new traits often arise already dimorphic, our study highlights the need for further studies on the developmental mechanisms of sexual dimorphism, how weapon traits covary within and between sexes, and the relative roles of different selective pressures in shaping weapon systems.

items.title: Contingency and determinism in rapid adaptation shape evolutionary rescue and extinction in Drosophila
items.blurb: Populations declining under anthropogenic stressors, including rising temperatures and novel chemicals, may depend on rapid adaptation to persist. Yet fundamental questions remain about what promotes and constrains such evolutionary rescue. We tracked demographic, phenotypic, and genomic dynamics in a replicated outdoor evolution experiment using Drosophila under insecticide stress, and also manipulated initial maladaptation by pre-adapting a subset of populations. Half of populations without pre-adaptation went extinct and, unexpectedly, extinction was associated with a greater magnitude of phenotypic and parallel genomic adaptation. Rescue was driven by polygenic adaptation that was parallel across replicates and not predictable from genes previously implicated in insecticide resistance, with notable genomic convergence towards pre-adapted populations. Targeted intervention through pre-adaptation prevented extinction entirely, despite evidence of pleiotropic costs. Without intervention, evolutionary rescue remains contingent even with exceptionally rapid adaptation.

items.title: Decline and extirpation of birds in a tropical Asian grassland ecosystem over the past century
items.blurb: Grasslands are facing unprecedented habitat loss due to settler-driven agriculture during colonial expansion, conversion to tree plantations, misclassification as wastelands, absorption into megadevelopment projects, and insufficient response to climate change. Globally, grassland birds have faced the steepest declines, with many formerly common species facing rapid decline, losing much of their original ranges. In South Asia, our knowledge of how these land-use changes in grasslands have affected birds remain scant. Natural history collections and archives are vital resources to identify historical baselines for conducting a resurvey and identifying trends in long-term biodiversity response. Yet such historical data remain insufficient in tropical regions. In this study, by compiling an unprecedented dataset of ornithological surveys from the 1900s using a diverse set of historical data, we conducted a 3-year resurvey in an Eastern Himalayan grassland first surveyed by British Ornithologist Herbert Stevens. We surveyed nine historical localities. Using a recently developed Bayesian method to calibrate modern surveys with historical museum data, we found a 70.5% decline in grassland specialist birds. We also report the local extirpation of four endemic species of grassland birds. Open habitat raptors showed a 74.9% decline, while generalist species showed an increase of 23.5% and wetland birds showed a marginal increase of 2.64%. By quantifying functional distinctiveness, a measure of morphological diversity, we find that loss of grassland species does not impact morphological and functional diversity in modern assemblage. We also find that most resurvey localities have a high number of invasive species that have completely altered these communities. Grassland specialist birds of South Asia are highly range-restricted and have specific habitat requirements; the lack of intact tall grass communities in concert with site-level disturbance pressures from grazing, conversion and fire have likely contributed to their local extirpation. Our study serves as one of the first efforts to resurvey wet grasslands of South Asia and document local-level extirpation. We also highlight the importance of museum-based research to document long-term changes for urgent conservation attention.

items.title: At base of ocean food chain, scientists uncover impacts of a changing atmosphere
items.blurb: Much of the concern about elevated levels of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere focuses on its effects on global warming as a greenhouse gas. But up to 30% of emitted carbon dioxide is absorbed by the oceans, where it reacts with water to lower pH and leads to ocean acidification, which has enormous effects on the chemistry and biology of marine ecosystems.

items.title: The 12th‑century Chinese poet who was among the first to explore the inner lives of cats
items.blurb: If you're reading this, then your media feed, like mine, is probably full of cats.

items.title: More than meets the eye: Refugee reception in eastern Germany can vary by group composition
items.blurb: Imagine a group of newcomers in your local area. Would you expect your neighbors to welcome them or react with reluctance? Would it make a difference how many men and women were in the group, or whether they appeared white or nonwhite?

items.title: Engineered gel controls particle release to help injured spinal cord cells recover in lab
items.blurb: Researchers at the FAMU-FSU College of Engineering have developed a gel that delivers therapeutic particles to injured spinal cord cells, a potential step toward new treatments for spinal cord injuries.

items.title: Why obesity affects men and women differently may be hiding in their fat
items.blurb: Scientists at the University of California, Riverside have uncovered a surprising reason why males and females may respond differently to obesity. In a study involving mice, researchers discovered that immune cells traditionally associated with allergies and asthma can either protect against obesity-related inflammation or contribute to harmful metabolic changes, depending on their type and biological sex.

items.title: Turning food waste into insect feed poses only low mad cow disease risk
items.blurb: Insects can convert food waste and by-products from the food industry (such as unsold ready meals or slaughter by-products) into ingredients for animal feed. In this way, they can contribute to the transition toward a circular food production system, in which what would otherwise be wasted is reused. However, these waste streams may contain animal proteins that pose a risk of transmitting diseases such as bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE), also known as mad cow disease. For this reason, rearing insects on waste streams containing animal proteins is not permitted in the European Union.

items.title: The Gulf's oil-eating microbes lay in wait before Deepwater Horizon spill, frozen samples suggest
items.blurb: A year before the Deepwater Horizon spill, a NOAA crew scooped up seawater from the Gulf and froze it. Sixteen years later, FIU biologist Shen Jean Lim tested it only to discover the microbes that devoured much of the oil in 2010 were nowhere to be found in 2009. So where did they come from?

items.title: Lasers near physical limits of miniaturization open possibilities for tracking life at the nanoscale
items.blurb: From tracking how cancer develops to exploring how the brain works, scientists need ways to observe biological processes at increasingly smaller scales. Beyond tracking how cells move and interact, researchers need to understand how tiny structures within cells, including organelles and molecular complexes, behave and change over time. However, identifying and tracking these microscopic targets individually remains a major challenge.

items.title: New model identifies priority areas for large-scale ecological restoration in Chile
items.blurb: Researchers from Chile's Institute of Ecology and Biodiversity (IEB) have developed a multiobjective model to identify priority areas for large-scale ecological restoration in Chile, South America. The tool integrates four ecological objectives: reducing species extinction risk, prioritizing carbon stocks, restoring riparian areas and assessing ecological feasibility. The findings show that including ecological feasibility changes restoration priorities, while 80.4% of the selected areas contribute to more than one ecological objective. By identifying areas where different priorities overlap, the model can help guide strategic restoration planning and support better-informed conservation decisions amid growing environmental challenges and limited resources.

items.title: New daisy genus named after botanist
items.blurb: Te Whare Wānanga o Waitaha | University of Canterbury (UC) botanist professor Pieter Pelser has been recognized with one of the highest honors in taxonomy, with a newly established South American daisy genus named Pelseria in acknowledgment of his decades-long contribution to studying the family tree of plants.

items.title: What Goes on in Our Brains When We See an AI Face
items.blurb: Deepfakes have jumped the uncanny valley

items.title: New Asian flying frog species identified in Indonesia
items.blurb: In the lush mountain rainforests of Indonesia, researchers have identified a new species of Asian flying frog with distinctive physical features, calls and unusual egg-laying habits. The discovery is described in a paper published in the journal Zootaxa by scientists from Museum Zoologicum Bogoriense in Indonesia, the University of California, Davis, and other collaborators.

items.title: Extreme cold preserves passion fruit's vitamin C, but not all of its antioxidants
items.blurb: Passion fruit can travel thousands of kilometers before it reaches international markets. Along the way, one of the food industry's biggest challenges is making sure its nutritional qualities survive processing, storage and transport.

items.title: Optimized supercomputer workflow accelerates protein-structure prediction
items.blurb: A Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL)-led team has harnessed the power of El Capitan to accelerate generation of predicted protein structures, drastically reducing the computing time required and opening new possibilities for drug discovery, biological research and national security applications.

items.title: Repurposed battery molecules drive key chemical reactions where oil meets water
items.blurb: The process of producing essential medicines and fine chemicals has long been powered by reactions involving intense heat, heavy-metal catalysts and hazardous hydrogen gas. Now, a team of Harvard chemists and engineers has demonstrated that these critical transformations can be driven cleanly by electricity, right at the boundary where oil and water meet.

items.title: Two proteins key to cellulose synthase trafficking and cell wall formation identified
items.blurb: A new study has identified Arabidopsis SNARE proteins VAMP726 and VAMP725 as key components of the trafficking of cellulose synthase (CESA), helping support the formation of both primary and secondary cell walls.

items.title: New platform improves accuracy of molecular counting in RNA-sequencing
items.blurb: The open-source platform, called UMIche (pronounced "you-me-kay"), is described in a new study published in Nature Communications. It addresses a common challenge in RNA-sequencing, where errors during sequencing can lead to inaccurate measurements of gene expression.

items.title: Gut microbiomes of endangered primates reveal hidden toll of habitat loss
items.blurb: As rainforests around the world are cleared for agriculture, livestock grazing, timber harvesting and development, habitat loss is pushing an increasing number of species toward extinction.

items.title: Rapid-scan satellite data offer clues to typhoon intensity
items.blurb: Between 1970 and 2019, tropical cyclones killed nearly 780,000 people worldwide and caused approximately $1.4 trillion in economic losses. As coastal populations continue to grow and climate continues to change, accurate forecasting is essential for saving lives and reducing economic damage.

items.title: GTA V flood simulations reveal how rising seas could reshape Los Santos
items.blurb: Grand Theft Auto V is one of the world's best-known video games. It is set in Los Santos, and although the city is fictional, its landscape and urban structure are modeled very closely on the American city of Los Angeles. Researchers from the Alfred Wegener Institute and the University of Potsdam have explored whether this virtual representation is detailed enough to realistically depict the consequences of a potential rise in sea levels and make them approachable.

items.title: Study uncovers molecular mechanism underlying lip-related floral organ curvature in slipper orchids
items.blurb: A research team from the South China Botanical Garden (SCBG) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences has uncovered a molecular regulatory mechanism that contributes to the development of curved floral organs associated with the distinctive lips of orchids, offering new insights into the development and evolution of floral forms in orchids. The study was published in New Phytologist on Nov. 6.

items.title: Prehistoric Humans May Have Hunted Hippos With Poisoned Spears
items.blurb: Peak Stone Age technology

items.title: We now know how radiation destroys electronics devices
items.blurb: A detailed picture of how a single particle of radiation can destroy a semiconductor device could offer pointers for how to make electronics more resilient to the harsh conditions of space

items.title: Woodcocks and Snipes: The Quintessential Odd Birds
items.blurb: They likely got odder after they “dropped off” onto islands

items.title: Meet the ‘celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness’
items.blurb: Nature, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03750-4 Astronomers report a rare pair of extremely bright black holes that were gobbling gas less than one billion years after the Big Bang.

items.title: Measles is back in the US: what worries scientists
items.blurb: Nature, Published online: 17 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03747-z Outbreak in the United States that has killed both adults and children increases risk of spread to other countries.

items.title: Prefoldin facilitates the action of FACT on macroH2A1-containing chromatin during transcription elongation
items.blurb: Prefoldin is one of the chaperone complexes that participate in protein homeostasis. Although it was initially described as a co-translational cochaperon that captures newly synthesized polypeptides and facilitates their folding by transferring them to class II chaperonins, nuclear functions have also been reported, including its contribution to transcription elongation and chromatin dynamics from budding yeast to mammalian cells. In this work, we have performed a proteomic search for prefoldin interactors in chromatin. Among others, we detected its physical association to FACT, the main histone chaperon that operates during transcription elongation. Lack of prefoldin provokes phenotypes associated to FACT perturbation, like chromatin-integrity defects in transcribed gene bodies, and derepression of cryptic transcription. It also leads to the specific alteration of FACT transcriptional dynamics in prefoldin-regulated genes. Lack of prefoldin also provokes co-transcriptional defects in histone dynamics, particularly in the eviction of macroH2A1, being this non-canonical histone a prefoldin-interactor itself. Finally, we show that these physical and functional connections with FACT and macroH2A1 respond to a single molecular phenomenon, and propose a model in which prefoldin would play a bridging role, enabling FACT to drive co-transcriptional eviction of macroH2A1-containing nucleosomes.

items.title: Semi-stability and unfolding of a KH domain modulate RNA binding and functions of MEX3A
items.blurb: MEX3A is essential for binding to Ago2/miR-126-5p and inhibition of apoptosis in endothelial cells implicated in cardiovascular health. Here, we discovered that the KH1 domain within the RNA binding region of MEX3A exists in equilibrium with an unfolded conformation. Using NMR spectroscopy and biophysical analysis, we dissect the KH1 folding kinetics and show that increased KH1 stability correlates with higher RNA affinity. The unfolded state of KH1 enables phosphorylation of T162, locking the domain in the unfolded conformation and enables recognition by 14-3-3 {zeta}. Residues in MEX3A KH1 that reduce its stability are located outside the RNA-binding interface and are evolutionary selected compared to human MEX3 paralogs. Semi-stability of KH domains in MEX3A and other multi-KH proteins may provide a general mechanism to tune RNA binding, enable phosphorylation and regulate biological function.

items.title: The dynamic expressome of Pseudomonas putida: condition-dependent remodelling of the RNA polymerase interactome
items.blurb: As in many bacteria, the 2{beta}{beta}'{omega} core RNA polymerase (RNAP) of Pseudomonas putida interacts in vivo with sigma factors, transcriptional regulators and auxiliary proteins whose relative abundance varies with the physiological state. Here, we used an in vivo immunocapture approach to examine condition-dependent changes in the RNAP interactome of P. putida KT2440. His-, Myc- and E-tags were separately introduced at the C-terminus of RpoC ({beta}'), a permissive, surface-exposed site accessible to cognate antibodies. Myc-tagged RNAP complexes were immunocaptured with magnetic beads and analyzed by LC-ESI-MS/MS and computational methods. The results revealed condition-dependent association of the RNAP core (RpoA, RpoB, RpoC and RpoZ) with distinct pools of sigma factors, as well as ribosomal proteins, RNA-processing factors and metabolic enzymes. Nutrient starvation, nutrient-rich growth and high temperature altered the composition and relative representation of RNAP-associated proteins. Despite the limited physiological conditions examined, our results support a model in which RNAP acts as a dynamic organizational hub of the bacterial expressome, integrating transcription with translation, RNA maturation and central metabolism.

items.title: Taxogenomic resolution of the 16SrIII (X-disease) group: elevation of Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni-related strains to species rank and proposal of three novel Candidatus species Candidatus Phytoplasma caryae sp. nov., Candidatus Phytoplasma conii sp. nov. and Candidatus Phytoplasma lactucae sp. nov.
items.blurb: Alongside the proposal of the taxon Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni for 16SrIII (X-Disease) group, the designation Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni-related strains was proposed for strains that were closely related to the taxon based on multilocus sequence characterization. However, recent genome-based studies have created taxonomic ambiguity by either assigning related strains directly to the taxon Ca. P. pruni or separating them into more than one genomic cluster without formal taxonomic classification or proposing new taxon for new divergent strains. In this study, we sequenced genomes of the pecan bunchy top phytoplasma (PBT), previously designated a Ca. P. pruni-related strain, initially to confirm the pathogen in an Oklahoma pecan orchard. Phylogenomic comparisons with previously sequenced Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni strains revealed four well-supported taxonomic groups based on average nucleotide identity, digital DNA-DNA hybridization, and phylogenetic analyses, with different host ecologies consistent with International Research Programme on Comparative Mycoplasmology (IRPCM) guidelines for assigning new taxon. Accordingly, we propose a reclassification of Ca. P. pruni and related strains into four species: Candidatus Phytoplasma pruni, representing the taxon associated with X-disease phytoplasma; three proposed new Candidatus species including Candidatus Phytoplasma caryae sp. nov, Candidatus Phytoplasma conii sp. nov and Candidatus Phytoplasma lactucae sp. nov. The study provides comparative-genomic insights into these taxonomic groups that support their evolution.

items.title: HDAC1/2 maintain TERT mRNA stability in TERT-rearranged neuroblastoma
items.blurb: Genomic TERT locus rearrangements define an aggressive high-risk neuroblastoma subgroup characterized by enhancer hijacking, high-level TERT expression and continuous telomerase activation. Although these structural alterations supply a strong transcriptional drive, the post-transcriptional mechanisms preserving TERT mRNA presence remain incompletely understood. We identified histone deacetylases 1 and 2 (HDAC1/2) as essential post-transcriptional guardians of TERT mRNA stability in TERT-rearranged neuroblastoma. Pharmacological inhibition or RNAi-mediated depletion of HDAC1 and HDAC2, but not HDACs 3-11, rapidly downregulated TERT transcript levels and suppressed telomerase enzymatic activity. Transcript decay kinetics following transcriptional arrest with actinomycin D confirmed that HDAC1/2 blockade accelerates TERT mRNA decay, reducing transcript half-life by 30-47%. High-resolution ChIP-seq profiling across the translocation breakpoint demonstrated HDAC inhibition does not alter local chromatin accessibility. Array-based DNA methylation profiling showed only a mild, non-specific global reduction in CpG island methylation upon panobinostat exposure and no focal correlation with TERT transcript loss across the breakpoint locus. Depleting TERT mRNA via HDAC1/2 inhibition dismantled a core 50-gene TERT-associated oncogenic expression network. Ectopic re-expression of TERT cDNA partially rescued cellular viability and normalized expression of key signature genes despite continuous HDAC inhibition. HDAC1/2 inhibition significantly attenuated tumor growth, reduced intratumor TERT expression and prolonging overall survival in both preventive and therapeutic TERT-rearranged xenograft mouse models. Our data establish a post-transcriptional rather than transcriptional mode of TERT regulation and confirm tumor suppression is partly driven by depleting TERT transcripts, uncovering a HDAC1/2 dependency in TERT-driven neuroblastoma. We provide a molecular rationale for therapeutic strategies disrupting HDAC1/2-mediated TERT mRNA stabilization.

items.title: From Calcium-dependent currents to Multitarget Therapy: A Pharmacological Strategy for Glioblastoma
items.blurb: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive primary brain tumor with limited treatment options and substantial interpatient heterogeneity. Ion transport and cell-volume regulation may represent pharmacological vulnerabilities in glioma stem cells (GSCs). Here, we characterized membrane currents in patient-derived GSCs, identifying a calcium-dependent anion conductance consistent with volume-regulated anion channels (VRACs) and an inward current consistent with Na+/Ca++ exchanger exchanger (NCX) activity. Based on these findings, we investigated individual compounds and developed a multitarget cocktail comprising niflumic acid (NFA), bumetanide (BTN), and R-ketorolac (R-K) to target complementary mechanisms involved in ion homeostasis, cell-volume regulation, and cellular dynamics. The cocktail affected cell viability and mechanical properties and showed synergistic effects in U87 cells and patient-derived GSCs with similar electrophysiological profiles. Treatment did not measurably alter spontaneous activity in cultured hippocampal neurons but caused substantial HMC3 cytotoxicity. Encapsulation in transferrin-functionalized liposomes attenuated HMC3 toxicity while preserving activity against glioblastoma cells, suggesting a potential strategy to improve treatment selectivity. Further pharmacological studies identified a potential vulnerability associated with NCX activity, although its contribution to cytotoxicity remains unclear. Overall, our findings highlight electrophysiological heterogeneity in patient-derived GSCs and support further investigation of ion transport as a therapeutic target in GBM. Combining multitarget pharmacology with targeted drug delivery may help address heterogeneous treatment responses, although further studies are needed to establish the underlying mechanisms, safety, and vivo efficacy.

items.title: statLens enables accurate and interpretable statistical intelligence
items.blurb: Diverse existing approaches and analyses of large-scale biomedical omics datasets along with the complexity of the corresponding statistical analytical workflows pose challenges to the direct application of large language models (LLMs) to data analysis tasks. We present statLens, a model-agnostic AI-driven statistical intelligence framework that integrates LLMs, code and human review. We demonstrate statLens using differential expression analysis across heterogeneous biomedical data as a use case. On 102 benchmark tasks from 74 datasets across six omics modalities, statLens maintained consistently high accuracy (92.5--95.0%) across seven language models and outperformed LLM-only inference (17.5--46.8%), whereas autonomous-agent accuracy varied widely (58.7--99.5%). We also showed that statLens substantially improved the accuracy of the four small language models (92.5--94.4%) over autonomous agents (58.7--92.2%) and LLM-only inference (17.5--43.5%). By decomposing analytical workflows into complementary tasks for code, LLMs and human experts, statLens provides an integrated framework for more accurate, interpretable and reproducible AI-assisted data analysis, particularly in complex omics settings.

items.title: SpaceMACE: Spatially-Aware Tumour Cell Annotation for Spatial Transcriptomics
items.blurb: Accurate discrimination between tumour and non-tumour cells is essential for interpreting spatial transcriptomics data and identifying spatially resolved therapeutic targets. Existing tumour-cell annotation approaches were primarily developed for single-cell RNA sequencing and do not explicitly incorporate the spatial organization of cells. Here, we introduce SpaceMACE, an extension of the MACE tumour-cell annotation framework for sequencing-based and imaging-based spatial transcriptomics. SpaceMACE first combines reference-based cell-type classification with copy-number-variation-based tumour classification. The resulting consensus annotations are subsequently refined using spatial proximity and gene-expression similarity. We evaluated SpaceMACE across multiple spatial transcriptomics platforms, including Stereo-seq, Visium HD, CosMx and Xenium, and across colorectal, hepatocellular and ovarian cancer datasets. SpaceMACE retained the high precision of the original MACE framework while improving the spatial coherence of tumour-cell annotations. Together, these results demonstrate that SpaceMACE provides a scalable and platform-independent framework for tumour-cell annotation in spatial transcriptomics and supports the spatial investigation of tumour-specific molecular targets.

items.title: Cell-state conditioning predicts the expression response to an unseen stimulus but not stimulus-dependent genetic effects
items.blurb: Second-generation sequence models can be conditioned on a cell state supplied as a single-cell snapshot rather than selected from a fixed catalogue, but whether that conditioning carries an experimentally applied perturbation has not been tested. We conditioned such a model on interferon-{beta}-stimulated and unstimulated monocytes from a published experiment, using cells disjoint from those providing the measurement, and asked whether the predicted expression response tracks the measured one and whether the same conditioning identifies expression QTL specific to the stimulated state. Predicted and measured responses agree at Spearman {rho} = 0.616 across 119 genes (95% CI 0.486 to 0.716), and at 0.607 after all 119 target genes are deleted from the conditioning input; across fifteen conditions the model's response scales with how much each condition's biology genuinely overlaps the target response (slope 0.73, Pearson 0.92), and a near-neighbour monocyte subset receives 0.295 against a measured overlap of 0.336. For stimulation-specific genetic effects we find no reliable evidence: the pre-specified primary arm moves from p = 0.0019 to 0.443 once both conditions must carry a measurable predicted effect, and the separation localises to the resting-condition baseline. Neither model generation's catalogue contains a perturbed sample, 0 of 4,430 tracks and 0 of 2,799 conditions, although both carry activation-state labels, so the gap is experimental perturbation rather than cell state. Two incidental findings apply beyond this model: credible-set membership mislabels over half of putatively condition-specific loci, and gating a ratio statistic on its larger term manufactures signal.

items.title: High-throughput identification of changes in cellular localization for RNA-binding proteins during adenovirus infection reveals viral harnessing of nuclear speckles
items.blurb: Adenovirus (AdV) is a human DNA virus reliant on host RNA processing machinery. While research into AdV has yielded landmark discoveries in RNA biology, studies investigating the scope of AdV dependency on specific host RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) are lacking. Here we performed optical pooled screening on a cell library where hundreds of RBPs are endogenously tagged. Pooled imaging followed by in situ barcode sequencing revealed a broad view of virus-induced host RBP relocalization patterns, including those recruited to viral replication compartments (VRCs). A targeted siRNA screen of relocalized RBPs demonstrated a requirement for the nuclear speckle (NS) core protein SON during virus infection. Depletion of SON resulted in reduced viral gene expression, impaired NS protein recruitment to early-stage VRCs, and impaired mobility of SRRM2 during infection. These findings suggest a crucial role of SON and NS functions in regulating viral gene expression and demonstrate the power of pooled tagging coupled to optical screening in investigating virus-host interactions.

items.title: Three-Dimensional Refractive Index Patterns Distinguish CD57-Defined Subsets of Human Memory T Cells
items.blurb: Distinguishing T-cell subsets is important for characterizing immune differentiation, but label-free classification is challenging because closely related subsets have overlapping biophysical properties. We combined holotomography with a three-dimensional convolutional neural network to classify primary human T cells from their refractive index (RI) tomograms. Fluorescence-activated cell sorting defined four reference populations: CD4+, naive CD8+, and CD57- and CD57+ memory CD8+ T cells. The FishNet-inspired classifier achieved 97.04% accuracy in a cell-level held-out test of 270 cells. Dedicated binary classifiers achieved 97.70% accuracy for naive versus CCR7- memory CD8+ cells and 94.44% for CD57- versus CD57+ memory CD8+ cells. Although the memory subsets overlapped in whole-cell descriptors, their volumetric RI patterns supported classification. These findings establish a basis for investigating intrinsic optical phenotypes associated with CD57-defined T-cell differentiation.

items.title: Integrated multi-omics reveals organ-specific jasmonate signaling in Arabidopsis under combined heat and phosphate starvation
items.blurb: Phosphate (Pi) limitation is a major constraint on plant productivity and is aggravated by heat stress. In nature, soil buffers air temperature, creating a vertical thermal gradient that shields roots from extreme heat; thus, heat and Pi starvation, although often co-occurring, are perceived mainly by different organs, shoots and roots respectively. How plants integrate these organ-specific stresses into a coordinated response remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated how Arabidopsis responds to combined Pi deficiency and elevated temperature, using a root-zone temperature gradient and an integrated analysis of ion accumulation, phytohormone levels and transcriptomic profiles in roots and shoots. The combined stress elicited a distinct response that cannot be explained by the addition of individual stress effects. Jasmonate levels changed in an organ-specific manner, with JA-Ile accumulating in roots and JA declining in shoots, and mutants with reduced (jar1-1) or constitutive (jazQ) JA signaling showed altered transcriptional, growth and leaf-temperature responses. These results identify jasmonic acid (JA) as a modulator of the balance between acclimation and growth under combined nutritional and thermal limitation, advancing our understanding of how plants cope with the multi-stress scenarios driven by climate change.

items.title: Role of Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) in muscle fatigue: significance for muscle myopathies
items.blurb: We report that Toll-like receptor 2 (TLR2) modulates skeletal muscle function. TLR2 ligands accelerated muscle fatigue development in isolated muscle fibers. Muscle fibers from TLR2 gene knock-out (TLR2-/-) mice were more fatigue resistant. This was not due to altered mitochondrial oxidative capacity or glycogen content. TLR2-/- muscle fibers had larger tetanic [Ca2+]i transients. Muscles from TLR2-/- mice had increased levels of Ca2+-binding proteins compared to WT muscles. Lastly, TLR2 was expressed in muscle fibers of control subjects and patients with idiopathic inflammatory myopathies (IIM), whereas high mobility group box protein (HMGB) 1, an endogenous activator of TLR2, was only detected in the cytoplasm of muscles from IIM patients. In conclusion, TLR2 signaling regulates force production in skeletal muscle. TLR2 and its endogenous ligand, HMGB1 likely contribute to the muscle weakness in IIM and, possibly, other muscle disorders. Therapies targeted to the TLR2 signaling pathway may counteract pathological muscle weakness.

items.title: Tissue-specific biotransformation shapes the toxicity of 6PPD-quinone in fish cell models
items.blurb: Acute mortality of salmonids exposed to urban runoff has been linked to 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q), a transformation product of the widely used tire antiozonant 6PPD. However, the cellular processes underlying 6PPD-Q toxicity remain poorly understood. Beyond the well-documented differences in species sensitivity, here we determined tissue-specific responses in rainbow trout (Oncorhynchus mykiss) cell lines exposed to 6PPD-Q: brain-derived cells (RTBrain) were more sensitive than gill-derived cells (RTgill-W1). To unravel the cellular mechanisms underlying such differential responses, we combined time-resolved 6PPD-Q cellular depletion kinetics, targeted biotransformation product (BTP) profiling, transporter inhibition experiments, and cytotoxicity assessments. Both cell models biotransformed 6PPD-Q, but RTBrain displayed a 6.6-fold higher cellular clearance rate than RTgill-W1. Chemical profiling identified four BTPs, including para-aryl-OH-6PPD-Q, which was selectively toxic to RTBrain but not RTgill-W1 cells. These findings reveal tissue-specific toxicokinetics as potential determinants of differential 6PPD-Q toxicity even within the same species. More broadly, this integrated approach highlights the importance of considering biotransformation and the production of biologically active transformation products when assessing susceptibility to emerging contaminants.

items.title: Measuring Phylogenetic Information Content Based on Clade Support
items.blurb: Phylogenetic information content is often understood as the degree to which data lend support to hypotheses about the monophyly of clades. This is most commonly expressed in terms of clade support, typically estimated by resampling techniques such as the bootstrap and the jackknife. Here, I discuss how to summarize this aspect of data quality. I show that raw bootstrap or jackknife proportions are unsuitable for this purpose and instead suggest a logarithmic transformation, which can be interpreted as translating the clade support values to the number of characters expected to give the same resampling proportion in parsimony analysis of a homoplasy-free data matrix. The distribution of the number of these "supporting characters" and descriptive statistics derived from this distribution, such as the mean (Mean Character Support, or MCS) and its standard deviation, provide powerful summaries of the quality of the underlying data set. I demonstrate for both empirical and simulated data sets that MCS accurately reflects information content, and that some popular alternative measures of data quality (the ensemble consistency index, the ensemble retention index, data decisiveness and the total support index) do not. Unlike most other measures of data quality, MCS can be applied to trees resulting from a range of alternative phylogenetic methods, including parsimony, distance and maximum likelihood approaches.

items.title: Policy-Enforced Genomic Repositories and Institutional Data Governance for African Pathogen Surveillance with UbuntuBio
items.blurb: Research centers curating pathogen sequence cohorts often operate under constrained bandwidth, multi-institutional data-sharing agreements, and strict biosafety requirements. Global public archives keep released sequences permanently open, external viral portals enforce terms outside local institutional custody, and standard Git Large File Storage (LFS) duplicates identical binaries across repositories without validating taxonomy or geography. We present UbuntuBio (v1.0.0), a Git-native, policy-enforced genomic repository platform deployed at https://ubuntubio.org and developed at the West African Centre for Cell Biology of Infectious Pathogens (WACCBIP), University of Ghana. UbuntuBio integrates four mechanisms under a single storage root: (1) bare Git repositories storing dataset cards, sample sheets, and approximately 130-byte LFS pointers backed by prefix-sharded SHA-256 content-addressed storage (CAS) with visibility-scoped wire deduplication; (2) a four-phase commit pipeline recoverable via cross-plane reconciliation that enforces 55 African Union country codes against offline Natural Earth polygons, core MIxS-derived fields, Taxon 9606 rejection, and server-keyed targeted human-marker screening identically across HTTP commits and Git pre-receive hooks; (3) institutional custody controls combining Data Use Agreements (DUAs), revocable 900-second RS256 capability tokens, key rotation, tamper-evident hash-chained logs, and externally anchorable RS256 audit checkpoints; and (4) an embedded SQLite WAL and FTS5 catalog filtered by access tier. In single-node evaluation, UbuntuBio classified 18/18 policy boundary fixtures consistently across Python, Git, and HTTP paths; showed 0/265,157 false cross-matches on 21/22 RefSeq pathogen sequences (while cross-matching Candida albicans 18S rDNA at 0.113% and Chlorocebus sabaeus Alu repeats in ENA stool reads, confirming targeted marker detection rather than verified human DNA decontamination); matched conditional uniform (n = 2,000; 200-seed 0.01% convergence 19.0% vs. 18.13% expected) and interior (n = 1,000) detection theory while detecting all spike-ins at [≥] 0.5% (30/30); halved two-repository disk usage on 613.83 MiB Nigerian E. coli runs; passed 27/27 structured-filter correctness checks over 10,000 biosamples and reached graded NDCG@10 = 0.920 on independent free-text BM25 queries with zero private leaks; and recovered cleanly across seven injected phase-transition faults.

items.title: KORUS: probabilistic ancestry inference beyond variant calls
items.blurb: Ancestry inference typically relies on variant calling and predefined population labels. We present KORUS, a probabilistic framework that infers ancestry from sequencing-derived k-mer representations constructed using ancestry-informative reference variants and encoded in Bloom filters, without requiring explicit variant calls for query genomes. KORUS separates genomic feature representation from ancestry decoding, enabling supervised classification, fractional ancestry inference, and unsupervised population structure discovery within a unified framework. Reference models were constructed from 643 genomes from the 1000 Genomes Project and the Simons Genome Diversity Project. Evaluation on an independent cohort of 22 whole-genome sequencing samples, with comparisons to ntRoot, SNVstory, and ADMIXTURE, showed recovery of continental-scale population structure, with supervised classification accuracy of 72.7-81.8% and ancestry-fraction concordance of R2 = 0.844-0.993 relative to ADMIXTURE and R2 = 0.665-0.983 relative to ntRoot. Ancestry estimates were consistent across alternative k-mer representations. Analyses of ancient human and archaic hominin genomes demonstrated that probabilistic projections quantify affinity to the learned feature space rather than necessarily indicating modern continental ancestry. KORUS provides a unified approach to ancestry inference directly from sequencing-derived representations and is freely available under the GPLv3 license at https://github.com/BirolLab/korus.

items.title: The pangenome of the Arctic picoeukaryote Micromonas polaris resolves cryptic ecotypes and identifies a polar-specific gene repertoire
items.blurb: Micromonas polaris is the dominant picoeukaryote of the Arctic Ocean, where it sustains primary production across habitats from sea ice to open water to the subsurface chlorophyll maximum. How a single species maintains this ecological breadth has remained unclear. Standard phylogenetic markers such as 18S rRNA are nearly invariant within M. polaris and conceal any internal genomic heterogeneity the species may possess. Here we present a pangenome of 14 M. polaris strains spanning the Arctic basin, integrated with Tara Oceans metagenomes, that resolves the species into two diverged ecotypes invisible to 18S rRNA but recovered consistently by prp8, genome-wide SNPs, ANI, and orthogroup-based phylogenies. The two ecotypes coexist sympatrically, with one lineage consistently enriched deeper in the water column across the basin. M. polaris carries 990 polar-specific hierarchical orthogroups absent from temperate Micromonas, organised around one-carbon metabolism, endocytosis, transmembrane transport, and photo-oxidative stress response. Several components show phylogenetic signatures of horizontal acquisition from co-occurring marine taxa. Atlantification is bringing temperate Micromonas into Arctic margins seasonally, but the polar night likely limits their year-round persistence. M. polaris and its polar-specific toolkit appear positioned to persist through the dark season, suggesting Arctic margins will undergo seasonal turnover rather than stable replacement.

items.title: Vertical transmission and community turnover in seed-borne microbiomes: lessons from an aMAIZEing model system
items.blurb: The seed microbiome represents a specialized ecological niche, governed by assembly processes that are only partially coupled to the surrounding soil community. While environmental recruitment and vertical transmission from the maternal plant are both recognized sources of seed-associated microorganisms, the mechanisms that determine their relative contributions and whether these contributions shift across generations remain poorly understood. Here, we used long-read metagenomic sequencing to track seed-borne bacterial community dynamics across a founding seed pool and two subsequent generations in two divergent maize (Zea mays L.) varieties exposed to contrasting organic and mineral fertilisation regimes. We recovered 112 medium- or high-quality metagenome-assembled genomes and combined MAG-level taxonomic and functional analyses with genus-level community profiling to characterize persistence and turnover dynamics within the seed microbiome. While soil taxonomic diversity was high, seed-associated communities showed a near-complete compositional disconnect from soil-dominant assemblages taxa, with a persistent Firmicutes core maintained across generations, consistent with vertical transmission. Priority effects remain a possible explanation for these patterns but were not directly tested. Genus-level source attribution suggested greater environmental recruitment under organic fertilization, with more diverse soil communities and a stronger contribution from the preceding seed generation under mineral fertilization. Seed-associated MAGs also carried genes associated with plant growth-promoting potential, although these detections could not be consistently linked to specific transmission routes. In contrast, maize genotype had no detectable effect on seed microbiome composition. Intergenerational persistence and environmental recruitment jointly shape seed-derived communities under contrasting fertilization regimes. Their relative contributions remain inferred from taxonomic overlap, and the effects of microbial source-pool diversity cannot be separated from the accompanying differences in soil chemistry in this design.

items.title: Maternal obesity disrupts glucose oxidation and mitochondrial fission in the myometrium at term gestation
items.blurb: Women with obesity experience delayed spontaneous labor onset, slow labor progression, and elevated risk of labor dystocia, but the underlying mechanisms are poorly understood.
