We previously established a mouse model of diet-induced obesity that exhibits decreased uterine contractility, labor dystocia, and elevated fatty acids in the myometrium. Here, we used this model to determine how maternal obesity affects energy production and mitochondrial homeostasis in the myometrium at term. Myometrium tissue and myometrial smooth muscle cells from diet-induced obese mice at term showed decreased pyruvate utilization, inhibition of glucose oxidation, and disruption of mitochondrial fission and mitophagy. Treatment with medium-chain fatty acids in both murine and human primary myometrial cells resulted in significant decreases in abundance of mitochondrial fission proteins. Finally, mitochondrial spare capacity in human myometrial cells decreased with body mass index of the patient providing the cells. Taken together, these findings indicate that fatty acid accumulation dysregulates energy metabolism and mitochondrial homeostasis in the myometrium and may contribute to dysfunctional labor in women with obesity.

items.title: GCase deficiency impairs uptake of α-synuclein-loaded ectosome by astrocytes
items.blurb: Parkinson's disease (PD) involves the prion-like propagation of -synuclein. One mechanism for the spread of -synuclein between neurons in PD is ectosomes. But PD is a multicellular disorder in which astrocytes also play a critical role. How astrocytes take up ectosomes and whether this is affected in PD is unclear. Here we show that GCase-deficiency, as occurs in PD, impairs astrocytic uptake of neuron-derived ectosomes containing -synuclein. The defect in ectosome uptake by astrocytes is driven by compromised macropinocytosis and can be rescued by reducing glucosylceramides or restoring lysosomal function. These findings identify sphingolipid metabolism as a key regulator of ectosome uptake by primary and iPSC-derived astrocytes. They also support a shift from the uptake and clearance of -synuclein by astrocytes in health, towards the transmission of -synuclein pathology towards neurons in PD.

items.title: Quiescent Cells Exhibit a Senescence-Like Secretory Phenotype
items.blurb: Cellular quiescence is traditionally considered a reversible state of cell cycle arrest, distinct from senescence, which is associated with a characteristic senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP). However, whether quiescent cells exhibit a comparable secretory program remains poorly understood. Here, we identify and characterize a Quiescence-Associated Secretory Phenotype (QASP) by integrating single-cell and bulk RNA sequencing datasets from human fibroblasts and preadipocytes. We find that quiescent cells exhibit increased expression of genes encoding inflammatory mediators and extracellular matrix-associated proteins, with substantial overlap between the QASP and SASP. This transcriptional program is highly heterogeneous, varying across cell types, quiescence induction methods, and environmental oxygen levels. In particular, contact inhibition induces a stronger inflammatory signature than serum withdrawal in several cellular contexts. Multiplexed cytokine profiling demonstrated active secretion of inflammatory mediators, including IL-1{beta}, IL-6, IL-15, and CCL2, in quiescent fibroblasts, with secretion levels varying by induction method and generally higher following contact inhibition than serum withdrawal. Analysis of single-cell transcriptomic data from human lung tissue further reveals increased QASP-associated gene expression in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF), particularly in myofibroblasts, linking this phenotype to inflammatory signaling and extracellular matrix remodeling. Together, these findings identify the QASP as a context-dependent secretory program that shares features with the SASP and may contribute to inflammatory signaling and extracellular matrix remodeling in both physiological and pathological conditions.

items.title: Three novel deep-branching orphan protist lineages from the marine rare biosphere
items.blurb: Metabarcoding has transformed our view of marine protist communities, yet many sequences in environmental surveys are not assigned confident taxonomic identity. These taxonomically ambiguous sequences may include lineages that are not within any known eukaryotic supergroup, which we refer to here as orphan lineages. These orphan lineages matter beyond taxonomy-based community analyses, because they can help us understand early eukaryotic evolution. Here we used phylogenetic inferences and sequence similarity networks (SSNs) of long-read metabarcoding data of the ribosomal operon (18S-28S rDNA) to identify three novel phylum-level orphan lineages. We designate these lineages Deep Orphan Lineages 1-3 (DEEPOLs) and show that they are exclusively marine and part of the rare biosphere, yet ecologically distinct: DEEPOL1 is a cosmopolitan generalist, DEEPOL2 a conditionally rare lineage capable of local polar blooms, and DEEPOL3 a non-polar lineage with a tendency toward the dark ocean. For DEEPOL2, lineage-specific digital PCR (dPCR) combined with catalyzed reporter deposition fluorescence in situ hybridization (CARD-FISH) provides the first in situ visualization of these cells, revealing small, flagellated, and morphologically inconspicuous protists. Together, our results show that substantial diversity remains hidden among rare lineages, and that long-read sequencing combined with targeted molecular and microscopy approaches offers a first step toward linking orphan sequences to organisms and their evolution and ecological roles.

items.title: Single-cell genomics reveals genomic and functional differentiation between freshwater and saline Achromatium populations.
items.blurb: Giant sulfur bacteria of the genus Achromatium reportedly contain extensive genomic diversity within individual cells. Most genomic data (35 assemblies) come from freshwater populations obtained from Lake Stechlin, Germany, alongside four single-cell genomes from a salt marsh and saline mineral springs. Here, we characterize marine Achromatium from mangrove sediments in Guadeloupe and compare them with freshwater and saline references. Microscopy, elemental mapping, and Raman spectroscopy revealed calcium-rich inclusions, and intracellular elemental sulfur as previously described for this genus. Scanning electron microscopy revealed two cell-size morphotypes. We generated eleven single-cell, four mixed-cell, and two metagenomic binned assemblies from Guadeloupe mangrove. Divergent copies of conserved marker genes revealed extensive intracellular genomic diversity in individual cells of both morphotypes. Multigene phylogenies provided separation between freshwater references and most genomes from saline environments, including the Guadeloupe population. Gene presence-absence analyses further revealed differences in functional potential between Guadeloupe and Stechlin cells across five functional annotation categories including PFAM, KEGG Orthologs, and CAZymes. Differences in genes associated with osmotic regulation, ion transport, carbohydrate degradation, and secretion systems suggest variation in functional potential related to environmental adaptation, interactions and resource utilization. No significant differences in functional potential between Guadeloupe morphotypes were found. Together, these marine genomes reveal genomic and functional differentiation from freshwater populations and suggest that intracellular diversity does not erase freshwater/saline population boundaries.

items.title: Biphasic glycocalyx remodelling balances immune cell recruitment and tissue damage during influenza infection
items.blurb: The endothelial glycocalyx is a glycan-rich barrier lining blood vessels that regulates immune cell recruitment, whose role in viral infection is unknown. Using a murine influenza model, we reveal that the lung endothelial glycocalyx undergoes coordinated biphasic remodelling: early shedding followed by substantial accumulation during peak immune activation. Genetic deletion of heparanase, the enzyme driving early glycocalyx shedding, reduced immune cell lung infiltration and improved host recovery. Conversely, using a new endothelial-specific glycocalyx depletion mouse model, we demonstrate that this glycocalyx accumulation actively limits immune cell recruitment and prevents excessive tissue damage. Together, these findings reveal that coordinated endothelial and immune cell glycocalyx remodelling is an active and previously unrecognised regulator of the balance between antiviral immune cell recruitment and tissue protection.

items.title: Gene expression in the hypothalamus of gonad-sex chromosome divergent embryonic chickens
items.blurb: Sexual differentiation of the brain of birds is shaped by gonadal steroid hormones and also by cell-autonomous mechanisms resulting from limited sex chromosome dosage compensation. In this study, we compare gene expression in the hypothalamus of gonad-sex chromosome divergent embryonic chickens treated with the aromatase inhibitor fadrozole to their control counterparts. Consistent with a lack of dosage compensation, we find a robust effect of sex chromosomes on hypothalamic gene expression, and a large portion of differentially expressed genes were on the Z and W sex chromosomes. Despite the presence of developing testes and markedly reduced estrogen concentrations in fadrozole-treated chromosomal female (ZW) birds, we find modest effects of gonadal hormones on gene expression in the brain. Weighted gene coexpression network analysis revealed that the most prominent effects were attributable to interactions between chromosomal sex and treatment. Our results highlight that chromosomal sex and steroid hormones together shape the sexual differentiation of the embryonic avian brain, challenging the primacy of the organizational effects of sex steroids on the brain during development.

items.title: A radial glial regulatory program bridges progenitor maintenance and neuronal identity
items.blurb: The cerebral cortex acquires its neuronal diversity through successive waves of neurogenesis. How molecular differences among early progenitors relate to their neuronal output remains unclear. Here, we identify a molecular program in early SOX9-high radial glia (S9RGs) that links progenitor maintenance with the regulation of genes associated with neuronal identity. Combining transcriptional and chromatin profiling with in vivo perturbations, we identify a program involving extracellular signaling, cell-cycle regulation, progenitor maintenance, and neurogenesis. We show that SOX9 regulates part of this program, including receptors that contribute to progenitor maintenance, while Notch acts upstream of Sox9 and reproduces several transcriptional and chromatin features of S9RGs. S9RGs express selected later-stage radial glial features and show distinct chromatin accessibility patterns at genes involved in progenitor maintenance, neurogenesis, and neuronal identity. Notch activation reproduces part of these changes, including differences at genes associated with lower- and upper-layer neuronal specification. Interestingly, S9RGs, which preferentially generate upper-layer neurons, share molecular features with the highly proliferative RG population in ferrets and with human outer RGs (oRGs) from cortical organoids, despite their different positions within the developing cortex. Together, our findings suggest that molecular differences among early radial glia could influence both how long they remain as progenitors and the neuronal identities they subsequently generate.

items.title: Genetic, neural and early-environmental architecture of resilience
items.blurb: Resilience is shaped by factors ranging from the genome through early-life experience to the brain, yet its biological basis in humans remains unclear because studies have rarely integrated these levels and have been confined to small samples. Using the Brief Resilience Scale (BRS) and multimodal data from tens of thousands of UK Biobank (UKB) participants, with replication in Generation Scotland (GS), we found that resting-state functional connectivity, particularly within the flexibility and valuation networks, is a robust neural correlate of resilience. Resilience also showed a generalizable genetic basis: a polygenic score (PGS) derived from a UKB genome-wide association study predicted BRS in GS. Genes and childhood experiences converged on the flexibility network through distinct routes: the polygenic association with resilience was partly explained by central executive-salience integration, whereas childhood experiences were associated with default-mode-centered integration. By separating genetically anchored from experience-sensitive routes, these findings point to network targets that interventions could tailor to the sources of an individual's vulnerability.

items.title: Neural reactivation of past events tracks narrative understanding as it unfolds
items.blurb: Understanding of episodic experience is not achieved at a single moment: it is a constructive process in which each new event is interpreted in light of relevant past events and prior knowledge. Yet this process is rarely measured as it unfolds, leaving unclear how the brain integrates past events to construct an evolving understanding of the present. We hypothesized that neural reactivation of past events at narrative event boundaries reflects not merely what people experience, but how they interpret their experience. We developed a behavioural paradigm that tracks, as a narrative unfolds, which past events people consider relevant for understanding each new event. By manipulating prior knowledge of the narrative's final plot twist, we examined the process by which the same experience yields different understanding. Across independent behavioural and fMRI cohorts, we found that prior knowledge similarly altered the variability and intersubject similarity of inferred relations between events and their neural reactivation at narrative event boundaries in the Default Mode Network. Moreover, stronger neural reactivation was associated with greater inferred relevance between events, and event pairs showing different behavioural relations across groups also showed corresponding differences in reactivation. These findings suggest that neural reactivation of past events at event boundaries reflects an unfolding inferential process that transforms shared experience into subjective understanding.

items.title: A temporal atlas of TDP-43 interactions reveals persistent network remodelling beyond stress granule clearance
items.blurb: Cytoplasmic aggregation of the nuclear protein TDP-43 is associated with several neurodegenerative disorders and may be promoted by cellular stress. However, the dynamics of TDP-43 protein-protein interactions during stress and recovery remain poorly understood. Here, we combined APEX2 proximity labelling with quantitative mass spectrometry to generate a temporal atlas of wild-type TDP-43 and pathology-mimicking TDP-43dNLS and TDP-43CTF variants. Interactomes were profiled across steady state, oxidative stress, and recovery. We reveal extensive state- and variant-dependent remodelling of TDP-43 interaction networks, uncovering distinct temporal interaction patterns throughout the stress response and recovery. Notably, distinct TDP-43 interaction signatures persisted after stress granule clearance, suggesting a molecular memory of stress. Together, our study establishes a comprehensive temporal resource for investigating TDP-43 interaction dynamics and provides a framework for understanding how stress-induced network alterations may contribute to TDP-43 proteinopathies.

items.title: Madden review – Nicolas Cage is a cartoonish NFL legend in David O Russell’s stinker
items.blurb:
Oscar-nominated director delivers a thoroughly unserious biopic, wasting Christian Bale and Sienna Miller’s talents

John Madden was a beloved American original, the burly football coach who segued easily from Super Bowl burnout to television darling to the last name in gaming as the NFL was overtaking baseball as the national pastime. When he wasn’t crashing into family rooms on football Sundays and Thanksgivings to break down the game’s rough complexities into fun-sized morsels, he was pressing flesh with everyday Americans while barnstorming the country in his Madden cruiser – the coach bus he depended on to compensate for his well-documented fear of flying.

That the Madden video game franchise outlived the avuncular Minnesotan, whose death at age 85 in 2021 was mourned throughout the sport, is as much a testament to his singular knack for teaching the game’s fundaments as it is to his willingness to bring his classroom to students, wherever they might huddle. But Madden, a new Amazon biopic that can’t decide whether it’s serious or slapstick, has drawn all the wrong lessons.

items.title: Theodore Zeldin obituary
items.blurb:
Revered historian, author and francophile with a novelistic approach to his subject

On the website the Oxford Muse, which the francophile Oxford historian Theodore Zeldin set up in 2001 to bring strangers together for mutually liberating conversations, there is a little section on dancing. “Few realise,” he wrote, “how important a part dancing has played in the history of freedom.”

During the French Revolution, 700 dance halls opened; in the 1830s, socialists liked dancing the galop because it involved changing partners; in 1968 (or thereabouts) women stopped letting men take the lead. “Dancing is like a carnival, freeing you from what you normally are,” Zeldin wrote. “Dancing together creates harmonies between people with different tastes. That is also what conversation seeks.”

I’m in the cinema foyer when I first spot them: hockey jerseys. Lots of them. “I’ve no idea what to expect!” giggles Chloe, who is wearing a black and yellow “Rozanov” jersey. Like me, she has never been to a 4DX screening before – but when Cineworld announced it would be showing episodes five and six of queer hockey drama Heated Rivalry in the novel format, she booked tickets immediately. “I actually had tickets for the 2D screening, but cancelled them for this,” she says.

Over the last two weeks, Heated Rivalry fans have been treated to big screen marathons of Jacob Tierney’s hit TV show, based on Rachel Reid’s bestselling book series, Game Changers. But 4DX is next level. The “extreme sensory” cinema technology is usually deployed for high-octane action flicks – films with epic battles or chase sequences. Still, with Cineworld offering the opportunity to “immerse yourself in the motion, wind, water [and] scent” of major league hockey’s raunchiest fictional romance, who could resist?

items.title: ‘Everything he said sounded like a song title!’ The rackety, romantic life of Bobby Charles, alligator-befriending bard of the bayou
items.blurb:
He was nearly an early rock’n’roll star but took a different path, from Fats Domino to the Band and pro-environment songwriting. As a career-spanning box set is released, those who knew him remember an American original

‘I was listening to Bob Dylan’s Theme Time radio show,” says Korey Richey, multi-instrumentalist with LCD Soundsystem, “and he said, ‘Bobby Charles is best known as a songwriter, but he has one of the most melodious voices ever transmuted into a piece of vinyl.’ I thought about it, and I agree: Bobby Charles was something else.”

Something else, indeed. Charles (1938–2010) was unable to play an instrument yet wrote songs sung by everyone from Fats Domino to Etta James to Kris Kristofferson. Signed to Chess Records in 1955 aged 17, he was on the verge of becoming a star at the dawn of rock’n’roll, but a preference for living reclusively – with a pet alligator – ensured he vanished from sight, and his music has long been unavailable. “He was a very strange guy, a loner,” says one of his Louisiana contemporaries, 88-year-old Johnnie Allan. “He knew what he had and wouldn’t compromise.” Now a box set, The Bobby Charles Story, containing almost every recording Charles released, aims to establish the Cajun magus as one of the greats.

items.title: We made GTA 6, the world’s biggest video game – we should have working conditions to match | Nestor Uriarte
items.blurb:
After the release of Grand Theft Auto VI this week, Rockstar employees like me can make history again. We need union recognition to safeguard our jobs

When I first got the call offering me a job at Rockstar, I was thrilled. I thought back to being a child and sneaking into my brother’s room to grab the PlayStation Portable so I could secretly play Grand Theft Auto: Vice City Stories. The same kid who fell in love with Rockstar’s games back then now gets to spend every day helping to create those worlds as an animation programmer at the studio in Edinburgh. This week, we will celebrate the culmination of more than a decade of effort: the release of the most anticipated game of all time, Grand Theft Auto VI.

But our team has the opportunity to make history a second time this month. Right now, the ballot is open for Rockstar employees to decide whether we want the union we have built with our colleagues to get recognition. As someone who cares deeply about our team, cares about what we do, and wants us to be able to keep delivering world-class games into the future, I’m voting yes.

items.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
items.blurb:
With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre

  • Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI?

In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone – that is the beauty of it.

For me, though, this game is about Jason and Lucia, the fugitive couple through whom you experience all that Leonida has to offer. Jason is muscular, handsome, ex-military, steady and unflappable, sincere but spare with words. Lucia has been boosting cars since the age of 14, has a wicked sense of humour and takes zero bullshit. (Lucia is the scarier one; I found myself turning much more quickly to violence when playing as her.) At the start, Lucia is incarcerated and Jason is making a go of things in the sunbeaten Keys, working for a dodgy guy down on the marina and renting a run-down house on stilts with a jetty round the back and a pet snake. When Lucia gets out of prison, the two of them try to make some kind of life for themselves – but before long they get caught up with the wrong people and have to flee the cosy life they’ve just started building.

items.title: ‘We want our story to be told’: inside a shocking 36-year fight for justice in Baltimore
items.blurb:
A staggering case of injustice is explored in the galling HBO documentary When a Witness Recants. The three subjects and producer Ta-Nehisi Coates explain how it unfolded

For most of his life, the writer Ta-Nehisi Coates would occasionally think of a chilling episode from his childhood in West Baltimore: almost exactly 43 years ago, on 18 November 1983, a 14-year-old boy named DeWitt Duckett was shot and killed in a hallway of Harlem Park junior high school in the middle of the afternoon, by an older teenager who stole his blue satin Georgetown jacket.

Coates was only eight at the time, too young to know the details, but old enough to perceive the collective horror around him. The sensational event – the first time a kid was killed inside a Baltimore public school, according to wall-to-wall local press – was a rupture in his child’s view of the world. “It was first time I had the sense that, oh, actually, I exist in a very dangerous world,” he told the Guardian. “And then you cut to the TV and it’s clear the rest of America is not existing in that dangerous world. The dangerous world is only for you and people who look like you.” Coates always assumed that the three teenage boys arrested and convicted for the murder were the right guys, and the episode faded into one of those strange imprints from the past, a blurry but foundational event.

items.title: Gjak by Dimosthenis Papamarkos review – sensational tales of wartime Greek struggle
items.blurb:
Translated into English in thrilling style, these interlinked stories of ambushes and vendettas vividly evoke the bitter conflict of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war

Nine interconnected tales about the violence of the 1919-22 Greco-Turkish war, and the struggles of its broken soldiers to reassimilate into civilian life, Gjak is something of a sensation. Originally written in Greek and Arvanitic, a dialect spoken by a Greco-Albanian ethnic group, and featuring characters from an unspecified Arvanite village, it was a hit in Greece in 2014 and comes to the UK in an agile translation by Siân Valvis. In her fascinating introductory note, Valvis writes of her attempt to capture the “unruly, galloping force” of Dimosthenis Papamarkos’s prose. She succeeds in thrilling style.

Delivered in a demotic, gossipy voice, these are rough-hewn stories of ambushes and vendettas, of brothers in arms being “closer than kin” and of lingering, sour regret. One of the translations of the eponymous Arvanitic word “gjak” is “blood” and indeed, graphic bloodiness is inescapable. Narrators don’t shy away from descriptions of how “shrapnel sliced [them] up like a fillet – eyes, teeth, ripped off half a jaw”.

items.title: From Dumb Starbucks to dada documentary: everything you need to know about Nathan Fielder
items.blurb:
With the UK release of You Can See Everything looming, now’s an ideal time to get up to speed on the bizarre, puckish and very meta comedic oeuvre of its star

“There are three sides to every story: your side, my side, and the truth. And no one is lying. Memories shared serve each differently.” Those words were spoken by film producer Robert Evans – but nobody has ever interrogated the idea more skilfully than comedian Nathan Fielder.

The three-hour documentary You Can See Everything – co-directed by and starring Fielder – opens in the UK on Friday, having already become an unlikely cultural phenomenon and box office sensation in the US. The film follows disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes in the weeks leading up to her beginning a prison sentence for defrauding investors; what emerges is a profound meditation on the nature of truth and the fundamental unknowability of other human beings. To view the film as being simply about the Theranos scandal is akin to considering Casablanca merely a movie about a nightclub. And, as one might expect given Fielder’s background, it’s hilarious.

items.title: The Man Who Broke Reality by Philip Ball review – the inspirational genius of Niels Bohr
items.blurb:
Scientific discoveries are effortlessly explained in this portrait of a man whose research was driven by passion

Niels Bohr shares with Albert Einstein pride of place in the pantheon of 20th-century science. The two had much in common. They were not expert mathematicians; they prized physical intuition over mere competence; and they did not shy away from the moral and political implications of their work.

But Bohr differed from Einstein in one crucial respect: his extraordinary personality. In his gripping biography Philip Ball ensures we feel the intense pull of Bohr’s genius. Today he would probably be considered neurodivergent; he possessed a passion for physics that cast a spell on all who knew him. Solving problems is the raison d’etre of any scientist, but Bohr went far beyond that: having inaugurated quantum mechanics with his model of the atom in 1913, he simply would not give up until the rest of it was understood.

items.title: ‘The aesthetics in my family were so high, I felt ugly’: Charlotte Gainsbourg on extremism, abortion and her mother, Jane Birkin
items.blurb:
In her new film, the actor plays a lawyer taking on the French state over reproductive rights. She talks about being criticised for her support of Israel and pushed to the limit by Lars von Trier

While she was making the film Women on Trial, about the real-life trial of a child prosecuted for having an abortion, someone sent Charlotte Gainsbourg a photograph of her mother at one of the pro-choice demonstrations that erupted in France at the time. It was “very moving”, says Gainsbourg to see her mother, the actor Jane Birkin, in 1972, “looking beautiful and in the middle of a demonstration”. At that time, in a court in Bobigny, a Paris suburb, the prominent lawyer Gisèle Halimi was defending 16-year-old Marie-Claire Chevalier, as well as her mother and two other women who helped her have an abortion, then illegal in France.

The Bobigny trial was new to her, says Gainsbourg, who plays Halimi, a leading figure in French feminism and activism who died in 2020. “I had no idea. For me, abortion rights started with Simone Veil” – the French minister of health who saw through decriminalisation three years later – “so I had to catch up.”

items.title: ‘Huge experiment in biogeography’: US offshore windfarms are creating artificial reefs

A few years ago, Tony DiLernia, a New York-based charter boat captain, heard rumors of prime fishing near the Block Island windfarm, off the tip of Long Island. So he went with his family to see for himself. Almost immediately after motoring up to one of the project’s five turbines, black sea bass and summer flounder started nibbling at his rod and reel.

DiLernia, who has fished for 50 years, wasn’t surprised: he knew about the reef effect, where certain species cluster around structures like the turbines. “It’s what we call ‘stupid fishing’,” he joked. “You’ve got this thousand-foot [signpost] sticking up out of the water saying: ‘Fish here.’”

items.title: The Guardian view on climate debt: a vicious cycle the world must break at Cop31 | Editorial
items.blurb:
Poor countries are paying creditors instead of preparing for climate disasters. The international financial system must stop deepening their vulnerability

The catastrophe that struck Nepal’s Himalayas in August began with a collapsing glacier. An avalanche of ice and rock unleashed deadly floods, sweeping away villages, bridges and roads, and leaving thousands dead or missing. It illustrated the dangers posed by global heating to the Himalayas’ increasingly unstable glaciers. Nepal lost a tenth of its electricity generation. Reconstruction will cost about $5bn. Yet the Loss and Damage Fund, hailed as a historic breakthrough at the 2022 UN climate summit, has earmarked just $20m for Nepal – less than 5% of the $482m that Kathmandu must pay its external public creditors this year.

“The scale of resources needs to increase,” Nepal’s delegation to this year’s UN climate conference drily observed. They are not the only ones agitating for change at Cop31. In its September report, Debt Fuels the Climate Crisis, ActionAid noted that the global south’s external borrowing is 100 times more than the climate finance it received. Poor nations end up trapped in debt dependency because they export cheap raw materials, but import expensive food, fuel and manufactured goods, invariably priced in dollars. The charity warned that climate-vulnerable countries are now expected to fund decarbonisation while servicing dollar loans that often pressure them to export fossil fuels rather than invest in green industrialisation.

Britain joins other signatories to statement urging introduction of targeted taxes on heavy emitters

The UK has signed a statement that backs levies on polluting sectors to pay for the impacts of the climate crisis, in a strong political signal that could pave the way for frequent flyer and crypto taxes.

Signing the statement at the UN climate summit means the UK joins a group of governments urging Cop31 to look at “the potential of targeted, small levies to ensure a contribution to the costs of climate action from polluting sectors”. The other signatories so far are Kenya, South Sudan, Spain, Timor Leste, Tuvalu and Vanuatu.

items.title: The reboot of poor Jensen Huang almost worked. But who can explain away 30 leather jackets? | Emma Brockes
items.blurb:
He seemed like the thinking person’s tech titan. But then came the affairs, the share collapse – and of course, the sorry items in his wardrobe

A few years ago, I attended a small dinner at a friend’s house in the US at which a tech billionaire was the guest of honour. He wasn’t one of the most famous tech billionaires – I’d never heard of him, although I used his communications platform every day. Nonetheless, it was exciting to get up close to someone that staggeringly rich to see if he was different from the rest of us.

And he was different, sort of. Leaning back in his chair, he seemed to suggest, in a bored kind of way, that in the event of a US standoff with Russia, Putin nuking London would be the sort of collateral damage Washington could tolerate. A bit of an odd thing to say to a stranger. He didn’t observe the usual rules of conversation but rather, like a Roman emperor waiting to be entertained, remained belligerently aloof.

Emma Brockes is a Guardian columnist

items.title: The corporate boom in vegan food is dead. Long live real plant-based cooking | Isobel Lewis
items.blurb:
The fad for plant-based junk food has run its course, but restaurants reflecting the centuries-long history of this cuisine still thrive

Have you ever gone to make a restaurant reservation and been met with a Google Maps listing bearing that harbinger of doom: “Permanently closed”? It’s a pretty deflating feeling – and one the UK’s vegan population knows well. Over the past few years, many once-beloved, plant-based establishments have shut up shop or moved away from brick-and-mortar businesses, from The Allotment in Manchester to The Vurger Co, which had restaurants in London and Brighton. Each shuttering galvanises the vegan community into supporting their local spots. But they’re gutting too, and deeply felt by a group who see themselves more as an ethically motivated community than simply clientele.

The so-called sorry state of the vegan restaurant scene has been widely reported on (not least by me). But after working with the food magazine Vittles on its inaugural London vegan guide, I have begun to challenge the “death of vegan dining” narrative that I had found myself perpetuating. And yes, a depressing number of my choices for the Vegan 99 closed while I was writing it; most recently, an omnivorous Malaysian restaurant with a walloping double-tofu laksa, which shut 24 hours before publication. But the process encouraged me to take a different viewpoint, instead focusing on the spots that had survived and the story they told.

Isobel Lewis is a freelance culture and lifestyle journalist

items.title: UNHCR Ukraine Operational Update - 18 November 2026
items.blurb:
Country: Ukraine
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

Please refer to the attached file.

OPERATIONAL CONTEXT & HIGHLIGHTS:

• Throughout October, the Russian Federation (RF) continued large-scale aerial attacks across Ukraine, increasingly targeting energy and other critical infrastructure as temperatures dropped and the winter season approached. Repeated attacks damaged energy facilities and disrupted electricity and water provision and other essential services, increasing risks for civilians during the cold season, particularly older people and persons with reduced mobility. According to the UN HRMMU, at least 372 civilians were killed and 1,981 injured in October 2026.

• Humanitarian operations are increasingly facing security challenges, with at least seven incidents affecting UNHCR partners while implementing UNHCR’s programmes in October. These included strikes impacting humanitarian personnel and operations, damage to humanitarian vehicles and partners’ premises, and repeated damage to interim evacuation points. While no fatalities were reported among UNHCR or partner personnel, the incidents underscore the volatile operational environment and continued risks to humanitarian activities.

• UNHCR supported the working visit of the delegation of the Ministry of Social Policy, Family and Unity of Ukraine (MoSP) to participate in the 77th session of the UNHCR Executive Committee (ExCom). Speaking at the ExCom session, Minister Uliutin underscored the importance of international humanitarian support to Ukraine, protection of internally displaced people (IDP) and investment in long-term solutions.

• In the fifth year since the start of the Russian full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and more than 12 years since the war began, UNHCR’s pro gramme in Ukraine increasingly aims to help war-affected people and displaced people to find durable solutions, particularly through housing and strategic protection advocacy.

items.title: WFP Ukraine Country Brief, November 2026 [EN/UK]
items.blurb:
Country: Ukraine
Source: World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached files.

HIGHLIGHTS:

  • WFP assisted an estimated 504,300 people across its activities in Ukraine in October, including 298,500 people provided with emergency food and cash assistance in frontline areas.
  • As Russian forces continued attacks across Ukrainian frontline and urban areas, October saw multiple incidents of hostilities impacting WFP and cooperating partner staff, assets, and infrastructure.
  • WFP and UNICEF have begun trialing integrated logistics and programme solutions in Kharkiv region, including shared warehousing and joint frontline deliveries

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Security Situation:

  • Russian attacks increase intensity in targeting Ukrainian energy infrastructure and focus on Kyiv city in multiple large-scale attacks, weakening the country and capital further as winter approaches.
  • In frontline and border areas, drone attacks against civilian vehicles, humanitarian movements and emergency services continued, including multiple instances of “double tap” strikes impacting emergency response, recovery and repair activities.
  • Repeated damage to critical infrastructure across central, eastern, southern and western regions of Ukraine is increasingly affecting the reliability of services supporting humanitarian operations beyond the immediate frontline.

WFP Impact:

  • The number of armed conflict incidents in Ukraine involving WFP or WFP cooperating partners this year (January – October) is already 81 percent higher than in 2025.
  • On 14 October, a WFP cooperating partner staff member of a was killed in an airstrike in the city of Sloviansk (Donetsk region).
  • The attack came just one day after a cooperating partner warehouse was attacked in Barvinokve (Kharkiv region) on 13 October, injuring two people and leading to the loss of 23 mt of WFP food.
  • In two separate incidents, two trucks belonging to WFP-supported bakeries were attacked by drones in Kherson region on 19 October.
  • Deteriorating security conditions in eastern Ukraine are increasingly limiting the willingness and ability of commercial transporters and humanitarian partners to access frontline areas. As such, WFP is increasingly leveraging its own delivery capacity to sustain humanitarian supply lines in frontline areas.

items.title: MSF Myanmar: Statement ahead of the ICJ ruling on Myanmar and genocide against the Rohingya
items.blurb:
Countries: Myanmar, Bangladesh, Malaysia
Source: Médecins Sans Frontières

Tomorrow’s ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ) will be the first time a judicial body will deliver judgment on whether Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people. This is a moment of special importance that has been long anticipated by Rohingya communities we have supported across the region for decades, including patients, colleagues, and our partners from Rohingya civil society in the diaspora. As a medical humanitarian organisation, we care for Rohingya patients in Bangladesh, Malaysia, and Myanmar — all of whom are affected by violence, displacement, and exclusion. For these patients, and for our Rohingya colleagues, recognition and justice matter. ​

In 2017, MSF published the results of a retrospective mortality survey conducted in refugee settlement camps in Bangladesh. The survey estimated that at least 9,000 Rohingya had died in Myanmar, in Rakhine state, between 25 August and 24 September. At least 71.7% of the reported deaths had been caused by violence, meaning at least 6,700 Rohingya, in the most conservative estimations, were estimated to have been killed during this brief period, including at least 730 children below the age of five years. ​

Almost 10 years later, we cannot ignore that these cycles of violence are not confined to the past. The current violence and deprivation being endured by Rohingya people is continuing to spiral. For those who remain in Rakhine State today, while the conflict dynamics are different from 2017, the crisis is ongoing: all communities are living through aerial bombardment and intense fighting between the Arakan Army and the Myanmar military, displacement, siege conditions, and the threat of forced recruitment as frontline reinforcements. For Rohingya communities specifically, long-standing discrimination and near-total restrictions on their freedom of movement compound the risks of the current conflict, leaving them particularly vulnerable to the consequences.

For those forcibly displaced across the region, they continue to face grave barriers to ensuring their safety, dignity, and access to healthcare. In Bangladesh, mass violence that erupted across the border in Myanmar in November 2023, and intensified again in April 2024, forcibly displaced 150,000 people. This brought the total number of Rohingya refugees in the Bangladesh camps to 1.2 million, placing further strain on already overburdened services. So far in 2026, more than 6,000 refugees arrived, citing forced recruitment, extortion, abduction of women and girls, land confiscation, and airstrikes as the reason for their attempt to reach safety in Bangladesh.

In Malaysia, harmful state policies leave many Rohingya at constant risk of arrest and indefinite detention, even when they are seeking medical care. At the same time, we are witnessing dangerous moves across the region toward so-called “voluntary repatriation” of refugees to Myanmar, despite conditions clearly remaining unsafe. Malaysia has already returned nearly 1,500 refugees from multiple ethnic groups, not only Rohingya. All of this is happening within a media and social media environment filled with hate speech towards Rohingya refugees, putting a target on their backs for public harassment wherever they turn. ​

Tomorrow is undoubtedly a landmark moment for Rohingya people. ​ However, it is imperative to remember that legal rulings do not resolve the immense medical and humanitarian needs that exist. There remains an urgent need for action from the Myanmar military and Arakan Army to respect international humanitarian law, immediately cease attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, and to facilitate rapid and unimpeded humanitarian assistance to those suffering the consequences. Crucially, states in the region must take action towards a zero-tolerance approach to public rhetorics of hatred, which continues to fuel violence against Rohingya refugees, driving people further away from healthcare, forcing people deeper into hiding, and in some cases, as witnessed by our team in Malaysia, pushing Rohingya people into psychiatric crisis.

The systematic persecution of Rohingya people did not end in 2017. They continue to be denied their most basic rights, including the citizenship they were stripped of in 1982. Practical, safe, and long-term solutions are urgently needed to end the physical and structural violence that, for decades, has denied Rohingya people the chance to live in safety, dignity, and freedom.

--ENDS--

items.title: A study of 26 due diligence systems in Ukraine shows how donors can reduce duplicate checks for civil society organisations
items.blurb:
Country: Ukraine
Source: Philanthropy in Ukraine

Please refer to the attached file.

Philanthropy in Ukraine compared 26 due diligence systems used by international donors and organisations. In 193 of 650 comparisons, one donor’s assessment already covers more than 80% of another donor’s requirements. This creates opportunities for donors to recognise each other’s assessments and reduce the administrative burden on Ukrainian civil society organisations.

Ukrainian civil society organisations working with several international donors often undergo a separate due diligence assessment for each partner. Donors frequently request the same documents and review the same aspects of an organisation’s work, yet organisations cannot always use the results of an earlier assessment in a subsequent one.

Philanthropy in Ukraine examined 26 due diligence systems used by donors and international organisations in Ukraine to see how much they overlap and whether partners could recognise each other’s assessments. The findings point to opportunities for recognition under existing systems. In some cases, donors could rely on a previous assessment for most or all of their requirements.

Donors assess similar areas at different levels of detail

The team analysed the documents and requirements of all 26 systems using a common framework of 60 criteria grouped into nine thematic areas. These include organisational governance, financial capacity, safeguarding, operational processes, partner management and requirements specific to Ukraine.

The study found substantial overlap. On average, each system covered 71% of the common criteria, and five criteria appeared in all 26 systems. The level of detail varied. Some donors ask a general question about a topic, while others require specific documents, procedures and supporting evidence.

Much of the duplication stems from the way donors set out similar requirements across different documents, templates and procedures.

In 193 comparisons, one assessment covers more than 80% of another donor’s requirements

To assess where donors could recognise each other’s results in practice, the team compared each system with every other system in both directions, for a total of 650 comparisons.

  • In 193 of 650 comparisons, one donor’s assessment covers more than 80% of the other donor’s requirements.
  • In these cases, the donor accepting the earlier assessment would typically need to check about five of the roughly 40 criteria in its own system.
  • In four of these directional comparisons, the earlier assessment covers all the receiving donor’s requirements.
  • 47 donor pairs show potential for mutual recognition at a 70% coverage threshold in both directions. Six pairs meet the stricter 80% threshold.

With mutual recognition, both donors could use the results of each other’s assessments. Systems that require a similar level of detail are the strongest candidates for this approach.

The figures indicate where recognition could be possible. Each organisation would still need to decide whether to accept another donor’s assessment.

How donors could make their assessments compatible

Based on the findings, Philanthropy in Ukraine proposes a due diligence passporting approach that would allow civil society organisations to use the results of a completed assessment when working with other donors.

A standard format for assessment results would show which requirements have already been met, which need further evidence and which fell outside the scope of the earlier assessment. Digital tools could match requirements across systems and transfer documents between formats. Experts would retain responsibility for the final assessment.

Putting the approach into practice would require agreements between donors, shared rules for recognising assessments, confidence in each other’s procedures and consent from civil society organisations to use their data.

The team also developed an interactive dashboard to make the findings easier to explore. Users can compare any two due diligence systems, see where their requirements overlap or differ, examine the level of detail and identify where recognition may be possible.

Read the full research report

items.title: World: How AI is helping to reinforce polio surveillance in Africa
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: Global Polio Eradication Initiative

**Brazzaville—** Every week, the polio eradication programme at the World Health Organization (WHO) Regional Office for Africa receives surveillance and operational data from the region’s 47 countries. From poliovirus detections and laboratory results to vaccination campaign coverage and health facility visits, this information is essential to guiding outbreak response and reaching every child. But with growing volumes of data spread across different platforms, turning information into actionable insights has not always been straightforward.

Until recently, producing a district-level map or country summary often involved several manual steps: locating datasets, cleaning and combining information, and generating maps, charts and reports. During an outbreak, teams could spend valuable time waiting for an analyst to provide the information they needed to make decisions.

The WHO Africa’s Geographic Information Systems (GIS) Centre is changing this through the integration of AI into its operational dashboards. Instead of navigating multiple databases or relying on technical expertise, programme officers can now ask questions in plain language and receive relevant maps, charts or tables directly from the dashboards.

For example, an officer can request a breakdown of circulating variant poliovirus type 2 (cVDPV2) detections by district in a specific country since January 2026. The system retrieves the relevant information and presents it in an accessible visual format, allowing users to explore trends by location, reporting period or virus type. The Poliovirus Detection Dashboard also features an AI-powered query function that generates written summaries from current and archived records, supported by relevant figures. This reduces the time spent on manual data extraction and reporting, allowing teams to focus more on interpreting findings, verifying information and following up on priority areas.

“AI-supported analysis is enabling the program to strengthen the monitoring of poliovirus detections and analysis of vaccination coverage and campaign quality while also enhancing surveillance monitoring through the Integrated Supportive Supervision (ISS) and eSURV Visits. By bringing together data across the different interventions, the program is able to identify potential surveillance gaps and identify areas with suboptimal campaign performance requiring closer attention and follow-up,” says Dr Kebba Touray, Head of the WHO Africa’s GIS Centre.

Similar capabilities are being extended to campaign monitoring, helping programme teams identify delayed supplementary immunization activities (SIAs), understand reported reasons for delays and address operational bottlenecks.

As the world marks GIS Day on 18 November, these innovations reflect how GIS is evolving beyond traditional mapping. By combining geographical information with AI-powered analysis, WHO AFRO is helping public health teams move from simply visualizing where cases occur to identifying patterns, understanding gaps and determining where action is needed most.

AI does not replace epidemiological expertise or human verification. Rather, it gives health professionals faster access to information, enabling them to make better-informed decisions and respond more effectively to public health threats.

This GIS Day, WHO Africa highlights the growing role of geospatial innovation in advancing polio eradication. Because behind every map, dataset and analysis is a shared objective: ensuring that the right information reaches the right people at the right time to help protect every child from polio.

items.title: Yemen: Yémen : au moins 64 enfants ont été tués et 64 autres blessés depuis l’intensification des hostilités il y a près de trois mois
items.blurb:
Country: Yemen
Source: UN Children's Fund

NEW YORK, le 18 novembre 2026 – Au moins 64 enfants ont été tués et 64 autres blessés au Yémen depuis l’intensification des hostilités le 3 septembre dernier. Ce bilan devrait encore s’alourdir alors que les combats se poursuivent aux abords de zones densément peuplées, notamment à Taëz et à Lahj.

« L’augmentation du nombre d’enfants tués et blessés au Yémen est bouleversante. Cela doit cesser », a déclaré Catherine Russell, Directrice générale de l’UNICEF. « Derrière chaque chiffre se cache un enfant dont la vie a été fauchée ou bouleversée à jamais. »

Les services essentiels et les infrastructures dont dépendent les enfants sont eux aussi directement touchés. Au moins sept écoles et 28 établissements de santé, dont cinq soutenus par l’UNICEF, ont été endommagés depuis le début de cette escalade. Le 2 novembre, une attaque contre le centre de santé d’Al-Suqyah à Lahj, soutenu par l’UNICEF et desservant environ 1 700 personnes, aurait par ailleurs fait cinq morts, dont trois professionnels de santé.

Parallèlement, les déplacements de population s’intensifient. Plus de 330 000 personnes, dont environ 174 000 enfants, ont été déplacées depuis la reprise des hostilités. De nombreuses familles trouvent refuge dans des bâtiments inachevés ou endommagés et peinent à accéder à la nourriture, à l’eau potable et aux soins de santé.

La situation dans la ville de Taëz est particulièrement alarmante. Alors que la route principale reliant Aden est fermée et que les itinéraires alternatifs sont peu sûrs, plus de 800 000 personnes étaient privées d’aide humanitaire à la fin du mois d’octobre, selon les informations disponibles. La production d’eau a chuté de près de 50 %, les prix des denrées alimentaires et du carburant ont plus que doublé, et les pénuries de médicaments, de carburant, d’oxygène médical et d’électricité perturbent fortement les soins d’urgence, ainsi que les soins maternels et néonatals.

Dans les zones touchées par l’escalade du conflit, plus de 1 160 écoles ont fermé leurs portes ou suspendu les cours, une situation qui affecte plus d’un demi-million d’élèves. Par ailleurs, près d’un enfant sur trois parmi ceux récemment examinés par les équipes mobiles de santé de l’UNICEF souffre de malnutrition aiguë. La surpopulation dans les sites d’accueil, le manque de latrines et l’accès limité à l’eau potable augmentent également le risque de propagation des maladies.

Face à ce contexte, l’UNICEF renforce son intervention d’urgence afin de venir en aide à près de 350 000 personnes. L’organisation redéploie des équipes mobiles de santé et de nutrition vers les sites d’accueil des personnes déplacées et les communautés touchées à Aden, Lahj, Abyan, Marib et Taëz, intensifie son soutien d’urgence en matière d’approvisionnement en eau et d’assainissement, fournit un soutien psychosocial et assure une prise en charge individualisée des cas, notamment pour les enfants non accompagnés ou séparés de leur famille.

« Les enfants au Yémen ont déjà beaucoup trop souffert. Il est urgent que les équipes humanitaires puissent les atteindre en toute sécurité et sans entrave », a ajouté Catherine Russell. « Toutes les parties doivent respecter les obligations mises à leur charge par le droit international. Les enfants doivent être protégés et pouvoir accéder aux services essentiels dont ils dépendent, notamment aux soins de santé, à l’éducation, à l’eau potable et à la nourriture. »

items.title: Somalia: Climate change pushing Somali farmers off their land, fuelling hunger crisis
items.blurb:
Country: Somalia
Source: Islamic Relief

Climate change is pushing farmers in Somalia off their land and into poverty, hunger and urban displacement camps, irrevocably changing traditional livelihoods.

With the El Niño climate phenomenon forecast to bring severe floods over the coming months, Islamic Relief is calling on world leaders at COP31, the annual global climate summit, to invest in protecting local agriculture and help farmers stay on their land.

Islamic Relief has interviewed farmers and displaced families across Somalia, who say their livelihoods are being permanently altered as increasingly extreme weather patterns make it harder than ever for them to keep farming.

This year’s El Niño is expected to be one of the most severe in decades and is projected to affect up to 3.4 million people in Somalia alone. Heavy rainfall and severe floods are forecast to devastate crops in a country where a quarter of people are already facing crisis levels of food insecurity. Almost two million children are expected to suffer from malnutrition by June 2027 unless action is taken.

One farmer in Balcad, Liiban Ali Mohamed, told Islamic Relief how El Niño could be the final straw after years of cumulative climate shocks have left him facing a precarious future:

“Over the past decade and a half I have watched climate shocks accelerate, with destructive flood years closely followed by severe drought years. We have experienced years when we waited for rain that never came, and other years when so much water rushed down the river that our farms were completely submerged.

“When you lose a harvest, you cannot easily recover what you spent. You have to start again from zero, even when you have no money left. Now, as we hear the news about potential El Niño flooding, I am deeply concerned. You prepare your land, invest your savings into seeds, and work hard every single day, only to lose everything to a sudden drought or a sudden flood.

“As a father, I constantly worry about whether I will be able to provide enough food. We need rain for our crops to grow, but we live in fear of having too much water at once. An El Niño flood doesn’t just wash away crops; it washes away our hard work and our family’s food security in a matter of hours.”

Islamic Relief spoke to other farmers near the Shabelle river, one of the country’s main water systems. The river is already at high risk of flooding due to increased rains upstream in Ethiopia, putting almost half a million people at risk of displacement.

Another farmer, Abdikadir Hassan Omar, said: “When floods strike, the damage ripple effect hits hard: families lose their primary food source, local markets face crop shortages, and income needed for medical care and school fees disappears.”

Muse Bufow said he has been farming for 12 years to provide for his children: “When the harvest is good, I sell the extra crops to pay for school fees and medicine. But when the season fails, my whole family suffers. My goal is simple: I want to keep farming, feed my seven children, and earn an honest living without living in fear of the next flood. We do not want to rely on aid; we want to work our land. With good irrigation, early flood warnings, and reliable seeds, we can protect our crops and secure a safer future for our children.”

The extreme weather events of recent years have pushed many families into destitution as crops have failed and livestock have died. They have been forced to leave their homes and land and move to crowded camps and cities where they have to depend on humanitarian aid.

Muna Mohamed Abdikadir, a 28-year-old mother of four children, fled her village in 2024 after consecutive failed harvests and the death of their livestock bankrupted the family. They now live in a camp for internally displaced people on the edge of Baidoa city. Her youngest child, 8 months old, is suffering from acute malnutrition.

“The hardest part of being a mother is watching your children go hungry when you have nothing left to give them. We left our home hoping for a better life, but here, even finding one meal a day is a struggle.”

Nafisa Abdirashiid Moalin also left her village for Baidoa after her husband died. Her 27-month-old son recently spent three weeks in hospital fighting persistent illness and acute malnutrition, and he still suffers from visible swelling in his face and legs. The family once made a living from farming but now she survives day-to-day by washing people’s clothes for a small fee. She said: “When my youngest son became sick, I was frightened because he is still very small. Seeing him admitted to hospital was painful. When I find clothes to wash, I can try to feed my children twice a day. When there is no work, we have to manage with just one meal.”

Islamic Relief’s country director in Somalia, Aliow Mohamed said:

“Our interviews with farmers in Somalia show how climate change is making it harder than ever for them to produce food and stay on their land. A single harvest determines whether a father can feed his children or pay for medical care, and when extreme weather wipes out a harvest the loss is felt by everyone. Too many families have been forced off their land and into camps where they rely on humanitarian aid to survive.

“Somalia is one of the lowest carbon emitters in the world, but its people are suffering some of the worst impacts of climate change. World leaders must protect their livelihoods and help them stay on their land.”

Islamic Relief is supporting farmers in Somalia through projects such as rehabilitating irrigation systems, strengthening flood early warning systems, providing drought resistant seeds, and teaching new agricultural techniques. Islamic Relief is also providing aid to displaced families in camps around Baidoa and Mogadishu.

items.title: La escalada del conflicto en Yemen, que se adentra ya en su tercer mes, deja al menos 64 niños y niñas muertos y otros 64 heridos
items.blurb:
Country: Yemen
Source: UN Children's Fund

NUEVA YORK, 18 de noviembre de 2026 – Desde que se intensificaron las hostilidades en Yemen el pasado 3 de septiembre, al menos 64 niños y niñas han muerto y otros 64 han resultado heridos. Es probable que el número de víctimas aumente a medida que continúan los combates en zonas densamente pobladas, especialmente en Taiz y Lahj.

“El aumento del número de niños y niñas muertos y heridos en Yemen es devastador. Hay que poner fin a esta situación cuanto antes”, declaró Catherine Russell, Directora Ejecutiva de UNICEF. “Detrás de cada cifra hay un niño o una niña cuya vida ha sido truncada o ha cambiado para siempre”.

Las infraestructuras y los servicios básicos de los que dependen los niños y niñas también se están viendo directamente afectados. Al menos siete escuelas y 28 centros de salud, entre ellos cinco que funcionan con ayuda de UNICEF, han sufrido daños desde que comenzó la escalada. El 2 de noviembre se informó de que un ataque contra el centro de salud Al-Suqyah, en Lahj, que funciona con ayuda de UNICEF y atiende a unas 1.700 personas, causó la muerte de cinco personas, entre ellas tres trabajadores sanitarios.

Al mismo tiempo, los desplazamientos se están acelerando. Más de 330.000 personas, entre las que se incluyen casi 174.000 niños y niñas, se han desplazado desde que comenzó la nueva escalada militar. Muchas familias desplazadas se están refugiando en edificios dañados o inacabados y tienen dificultades para obtener alimentos y agua potable, así como para acceder a la atención sanitaria.

La situación es especialmente alarmante en la ciudad de Taiz. Debido a que la principal carretera que la conecta con Adén está cerrada y las rutas alternativas son inseguras, a finales de octubre más de 800.000 personas carecían de acceso a la asistencia humanitaria, según la información disponible. La producción de agua ha disminuido cerca de un 50%, los precios de los alimentos y el combustible se han duplicado con creces y la escasez de medicamentos, combustible, oxígeno medicinal y electricidad están poniendo en peligro la atención materna, neonatal y de emergencia.

En las zonas afectadas por la escalada del conflicto, más de 1.160 escuelas han cerrado o han suspendido las clases, lo que ha interrumpido la educación de más de medio millón de estudiantes. Además, los equipos móviles de salud de UNICEF han detectado desnutrición aguda en aproximadamente uno de cada tres niños y niñas examinados recientemente. El hacinamiento en los campamentos de desplazados, la escasez de letrinas y el acceso limitado al agua potable también están aumentando el riesgo de enfermedad.

UNICEF está ampliando su respuesta de emergencia y prevé llegar a 350.000 personas. Para ello, está redesplegando equipos móviles de salud y nutrición en los campamentos para personas desplazadas y las comunidades afectadas de Adén, Lahj, Abyan, Marib y Taiz; está aumentando la ayuda de emergencia en materia de agua y saneamiento y está brindando apoyo psicosocial y gestión de casos para niños y niñas, incluidos aquellos que no están acompañados o a los que se ha separado de sus familias.

“Los niños y niñas de Yemen están sufriendo mucho. Necesitamos urgentemente un acceso humanitario seguro y sin trabas”, aseguró Russell. “Todas las partes deben cumplir con sus obligaciones en virtud del derecho internacional. Deben proteger a los niños y niñas y garantizar su acceso a bienes y servicios esenciales, en particular la atención sanitaria, la educación, el agua potable y la comida”.

items.title: Ukraine: From reactive response to a culture of care [EN/UK]
items.blurb:
Country: Ukraine
Source: Prosper Global

Please refer to the attached files.

Institutionalizing Duty of Care for local partners in Ukraine

Local organizations deliver a large share of the humanitarian response in Ukraine, often closest to the front line and with the fewest protections. This report documents how Prosper Global (formerly Mercy Corps) in Ukraine moved from ad hoc, reactive support to an institutionalized Duty of Care Minimum Package for its local partners between 2022 and 2025. It sets out the nine options available to partners, how the package was embedded into partnership systems, what partners prioritized and which gaps remain. Key takeaway is that Duty of Care for partners works best when it is non-negotiable as a standard, yet flexible, risk-based and partner-led in its application.

Why Duty of Care matters

Humanitarian work in Ukraine is carried out under persistent threat. Aid workers and volunteers operate within range of artillery, missiles and drones. Offices and homes are damaged in attacks on cities far from the front line, and repeated strikes on energy infrastructure leave teams without power, heating and connectivity for hours or days. Constant air-raid alerts add a layer of cumulative stress that rarely disappears.

Local civil society organizations carry a disproportionate share of this risk. They are often the first to reach affected communities and the last to leave, yet they typically work with small teams, mixed employment arrangements and limited access to insurance, security expertise or psychosocial support. Shifting leadership to local actors without ensuring their protection transfers risk rather than power.

Prosper Global works in Ukraine primarily through partnerships, collaborating with around 35 local partners across humanitarian response, economic recovery, agriculture and energy resilience. A partner organization is not an aid-delivery channel but a community of professionals whose safety and well-being are integral to the success of the humanitarian mission.

items.title: South Sudan - Concept of Operations, November 2026
items.blurb:
Country: South Sudan
Sources: Logistics Cluster, World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached file.

Summary

Humanitarian logistics operations in South Sudan continue to face significant access constraints driven by inadequate road infrastructure, seasonal flooding, insecurity and deterioration of key supply routes. Renewed conflict and localized insecurity further disrupt humanitarian supply chains, while much of the road network remains unpaved and highly vulnerable to seasonal deterioration. During the rainy season, critical routes frequently become impassable, resulting in delivery delays, higher transport costs and increased reliance on costlier alternative transport modalities. These constraints are particularly acute in Jonglei, Unity and Upper Nile, where poor road conditions, flooding and insecurity continue to restrict last-mile delivery to vulnerable and hard-to-reach communities. Despite ongoing improvements by humanitarian, government and private-sector actors, significant access gaps persist, underscoring the need for sustained donor investment in early prepositioning, coordinated access planning, critical route rehabilitation and maintenance, and common logistics services to improve cost-efficiency, reduce supply disruptions and ensure timely delivery of life-saving assistance.

items.title: IOM Yemen Dispatch October 2026
items.blurb:
Country: Yemen
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Yemen’s security and humanitarian crisis worsened in October with the expanding ground offensives, intensifying cross-border air strikes, and severe strains on already fragile structures for essential services such as healthcare. Ansar Allah (AA) forces sustained their multi-axis offensives across southwestern fronts, continuing heavy assaults on the key frontlines in Taiz while launching multiple strikes at strategic structures including the Presidential Palace and International Airport in Aden. This led to large-scale movements, driving the cumulative number of newly displaced individuals to over 300,000 since June. Taiz became the main frontline and humanitarian concern when AA forces captured Al-Turbah and AsSafiyah, cutting the main Taiz–Aden Road and effectively encircling Taiz City. Key commercial and humanitarian transport corridors remained blocked or compromised, with severe access restrictions critically isolating the population in Taiz. AA forces expanded long-range ballistic missile and drone strikes against the International Airports, oil infrastructures, and military installations across Saudi Arabia, and Saudi-led coalition forces alongside the Government of Yemen (GoY) also intensified air strikes against key AA positions in Yemen. As of 27 October, OHCHR had documented 263 civilian casualties, including 67 people killed. Children accounted for 97 of the casualties and about half of those killed. With the surge in conflict casualties, major referral hospitals across Taiz, Lahj, Marib, and Hadramawt faced severe shortages of basic medical supplies, fuel, and medical oxygen, and were forced to suspend routine and elective care to prioritize trauma operations. The health emergency was compounded by damaged water treatment systems and overcrowded, unsanitary conditions in displacement sites across the top concentrated governorates such as Lahj, Abyan, Taiz, and Aden. Food security exacerbated as staple commodities and fuel prices increased steeply with the continuing supply chain blockades and worsening access situation. Depleted humanitarian stockpiles and severe underfunding raise concerns of acute malnutrition cases increasing, as estimated 5.4 million people in GoY-controlled areas are expected to be in IPC Phase 3 or worse food insecurity in the final quarter of the year. Both GoY and AA raised fuel prices in their respective areas of control in the last week of October, with official price of gasoline ranging between YR 570 per liter (AA-controlled area, 20% increase since midSeptember), YR 1,700 per liter (GoY-controlled area), and over YR 2,500 per liter in Taiz. The citizens are forced to purchase fuel in the black market, where petrol prices skyrocketed to over YR 150,000 for a 20-liter can, as most gas stations have shut down. Water production in Taiz city has fallen by about half due to the critical shortage of fuel.

items.title: IOM Yemen Dispatch Situation Overview September 2026
items.blurb:
Country: Yemen
Source: International Organization for Migration

Please refer to the attached file.

SITUATION OVERVIEW

Yemen’s security and humanitarian situation worsened significantly throughout September, driven by the continued spread of ground fighting following August’s violent escalations. Ground hostilities expanded rapidly across southwestern fronts, with Ansar Allah (AA) forces intensifying offensives in Ta’iz and Lahj as they attempted to consolidate gains on the West Coast by securing the overlooking mountains. The fighting triggered a massive surge in displacement, forcing over 160,140 individuals to flee their homes, particularly from the Maqbanah, Jabal Habashi, and Al Ma’afer districts in Ta’iz. Vital supply lines, including the crucial road linking Mokha to Ta’iz City, were severely disrupted and cut off, stranding communities and impacting humanitarian access. The AA forces claimed to have targeted several sites in Riyadh and the Aramco facilities in Yanbu, a Saudi Red Sea port, with missiles and drones. Saudi Arabia requested air defenses for critical facilities from Egypt, France, Pakistan, and the UK. French President Emmanuel Macron said France would send military assets to help protect Yanbu following the attack, as the concerns over maritime security and global oil prices grew. Saudi Arabia also reportedly urged the Government of Yemen (GoY) to call for a general mobilization, which was announced in a speech marking the anniversary of the September 26 Revolution. On the other side, in a move to capitalize on its capture of the Bab al-Mandeb and the West Coast, the AA-affiliated Red Sea Ports and Tax Customs Authorities announced reductions in vessel and container fees and port taxes, effective 1 October. The sharp escalation in violence severely strained Yemen’s already compromised health infrastructure, with hospitals in Ta’iz, Ma’rib, and Hadramaut overwhelmed by casualties. Major health centers were forced to suspend non-emergency care—such as maternity and obstetrics services—to reallocate scarce beds and medical personnel toward trauma management. The cholera epidemic maintained a strong hold across southern and western governorates, with transmission exacerbated by population displacement and damaged water and sanitation infrastructure. Abyan and Lahj continued to report the highest concentration of suspected cases, while newly displaced clusters in Ta’iz and Aden saw rising incidence rates. According to the IPC, nearly five million people faced crisis levels of hunger or worse in government-controlled areas between March and May, including 1.4 million in emergency conditions, and it has been observed that food security has significantly deteriorated since the escalation began. Wheat flour prices increased by 10 per cent in parts of Ta’iz as of late September, while traders estimate wheat stocks will cover only about two months of demand. At the UN General Assembly, 80 countries supported a statement condemning “the Houthis’ decision to resume the conflict in Yemen, their continuous strikes on Saudi Arabia, and their reckless attacks on the Red Sea.” UN Special Envoy Hans Grundberg met with AA negotiators in Muscat to avoid further escalation and held talks in Cairo with the regional powers, including Egypt and the League of Arab States.
