EU opens new chapter in its relations with Syria

Quote(s)

A peaceful, stable and inclusive Syria is important for Syrians, to the region and to Europe. The EU is ready to deepen its partnership with Syria as Syrians rebuild their country for all citizens. At today’s Forum in Damascus, we focused on what international partners and businesses can do to support the country’s own priorities, so people can find jobs, businesses can reopen and services can further be restored.

Dubravka Šuica, Commissioner for the Mediterranean

items.title: Humanitarian Coordinator calls for strengthened Ebola readiness in South Sudan
items.blurb:
Country: South Sudan
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

Juba, 17 November 2026 – The United Nations Resident Coordinator and Humanitarian Coordinator in South Sudan, Mr. Ramanathan Balakrishnan, has called for increased preparedness and readiness to respond to a potential Ebola virus disease (EVD) outbreak in the country.

The call follows a recent full-scale simulation exercise conducted in October 2026 by the Ministry of Health, the National Public Health Institute (NPHI), the World Health Organization (WHO) and partners to assess the country's capacity to detect, notify, investigate and respond to a potential EVD outbreak.

The exercise assessed key areas of South Sudan’s Ebola preparedness efforts, including case management, infection prevention and control, laboratory capacity, contact tracing and coordination. While the exercise demonstrated the system’s capacity to quickly detect simulated cases, significant gaps remain in alert management, rapid response team management, health worker remuneration, ambulance services, laboratory facilities, personal protective equipment supplies, contact tracing, and screening arrangements at points of entry.

To address these challenges, the Humanitarian Coordinator has launched a three-month prioritised plan to mobilise financial resources to address the operational and capacity gaps identified during the simulation exercise. He called on donors and partners to support the plan, which requests USD$7 million to strengthen preparedness and response capacities.

“While there are no reported cases of Ebola in South Sudan, closing these preparedness gaps is critical to ensure that South Sudan is better prepared to detect, contain and respond to a potential outbreak, and to protect the lives and well-being of its people,” Mr. Balakrishnan said.

Reiterating the importance of national government leadership in strengthening EVD preparedness, Mr. Balakrishnan said, “The payment of health worker salaries by the government authorities is critical, as is facilitating access for Ebola-related movements for both health actors and UNMISS and ensuring the safety and security of humanitarian workers.”

items.title: World: ACNUR presenta un nuevo portal de datos sobre refugiados para reforzar la evidencia e impulsar soluciones para millones de personas desplazadas
items.blurb:
Country: World
Source: UN High Commissioner for Refugees

GINEBRA – En un momento en el que la información fragmentada y la narrativa sesgada sobre el desplazamiento forzado corren el riesgo de influir en decisiones que afectan a millones de personas, ACNUR, la Agencia de la ONU para los Refugiados, presentó hoy su nuevo Portal de Datos sobre refugiados, un punto de acceso único y abierto a datos fiables y verificados sobre personas refugiadas, desplazadas por la fuerza y apátridas.

Por primera vez, el portal recopila estadísticas demográficas junto con información sobre las condiciones de vida, las necesidades de protección y la situación socioeconómica de las personas desplazadas, ofreciendo una visión más completa del desplazamiento, su magnitud, los retos a los que se enfrentan las personas y los avances que se están logrando hacia la búsqueda de soluciones.

Desde datos sobre la pobreza y la matriculación escolar hasta la nutrición, el acceso al agua potable y otros indicadores de bienestar, el portal ofrece una visión más amplia de lo que significa que una persona esté desplazada.

“Detrás de cada dato hay una persona, una experiencia vivida y un futuro. Disponer de datos fiables es esencial para garantizar que las decisiones que tomamos protejan la seguridad de las personas, respeten su dignidad y les brinden oportunidades para prosperar”, afirmó Edem Wosornu, Alta Comisionada Auxiliar para la Protección de ACNUR.

En consonancia con la visión “50 para 35” de ACNUR, cuyo objetivo es reducir a la mitad el número de personas desplazadas por la fuerza que dependen de la asistencia humanitaria para 2035, esta base empírica más amplia ayudará a los gobiernos, a los socios para el desarrollo y a las organizaciones humanitarias a medir los avances hacia la autosuficiencia y las soluciones, evaluar si las políticas y los programas están mejorando la vida de los refugiados, identificar las desigualdades persistentes y las deficiencias operativas, y determinar dónde se necesitan más medidas e inversiones.

Por ejemplo, los datos comparables sobre pobreza disponibles a través del portal para diez países muestran que las tasas de pobreza entre las personas refugiadas superan sistemáticamente a las de las comunidades de acogida, oscilando entre alrededor del 10 por ciento y más del 90 por ciento en los datos recopilados entre 2018 y 2024.

Gracias a una experiencia de usuario moderna e integrada, el Portal de Datos sobre refugiados de ACNUR permitirá a los usuarios explorar, acceder, reutilizar e integrar los datos en sus propios análisis, informes y procesos de toma de decisiones.

Periodistas e investigadores pueden recurrir a información fiable para investigar tendencias, situar las cifras de desplazamiento en su contexto, y elaborar reportajes y análisis basados en pruebas. El nuevo portal permitirá la integración de los datos sobre desplazamiento en sus otras plataformas, mapas, informes y herramientas digitales a través de interfaces de programación de aplicaciones (API) abiertas.

El portal también está diseñado para funcionar con otras plataformas de datos, incluido el Sistema de Datos Comunes de las Naciones Unidas, lo que crea oportunidades para conectar datos sobre personas refugiadas con estadísticas de desarrollo más amplias y comparar las circunstancias de los refugiados con las del conjunto de la población en ámbitos como educación, empleo, salud, financiación y otros aspectos de la vida.

El lanzamiento del portal también supone un paso importante en la transformación digital más amplia de ACNUR. Mediante la consolidación de sistemas de datos fragmentados y la adopción de estándares de datos modernos, la automatización y la inteligencia artificial, la organización pretende que su infraestructura de datos sea más predictiva, eficiente y capaz de responder a las necesidades actuales.

“No se trata solo de una actualización tecnológica, sino de una inversión estratégica en un enfoque más sostenible, adaptable y eficiente de la gestión de datos, que reduce la fragmentación y facilita el mantenimiento, el desarrollo y la mejora de los sistemas a lo largo del tiempo”, afirmó Wosornu. “En última instancia, el Portal de Datos sobre refugiados de ACNUR se basa en una convicción sencilla pero poderosa: la información fiable puede cambiar la forma en que el mundo entiende el desplazamiento y cómo responde ante el”.

Al situar los datos y las pruebas fiables en el centro del debate mundial sobre el desplazamiento forzado, ACNUR pretende reforzar la confianza, respaldar políticas e inversiones más eficaces y contribuir a que una comprensión más profunda del desplazamiento se traduzca en acciones duraderas y significativas.

El Portal de Datos sobre refugiados se ha desarrollado con el apoyo del Centro Conjunto de Datos sobre Desplazamiento Forzado del Banco Mundial y ACNUR.

Nota para editoras y editores:

La versión actual del Portal de Datos sobre refugiados incluye un conjunto limitado de funciones y contenidos. La plataforma seguirá desarrollándose en 2027 y, con el tiempo, se irán añadiendo conjuntos de datos, páginas por país y contenidos temáticos adicionales. Como parte de este proceso, los portales de datos existentes de ACNUR se irán retirando progresivamente en los próximos meses.

items.title: Trees Alone Cannot Protect Wildlife: Chandigarh Survey Shows Why Grasslands & Wetlands Matter Too
items.blurb: Take a walk through a city park. There are trees lining the paths, lawns stretching between them and plenty of shade. It looks green, perhaps even thriving. But where are the wild grasses that feed grazing animals? The flowering shrubs that attract butterflies? The ponds and stream banks where birds and other creatures find food and shelter? A place can look green while losing what wildlife needs to survive. That is the message emerging from Chandigarh’s 2026 wildlife survey. Researchers recorded an impressive range of species, from a leopard and sambar deer to birds and butterflies. Yet they also found that several native trees were struggling to regenerate naturally and recommended greater protection for grasslands, wetlands and other habitats. For Indian cities, where planting drives often signal environmental progress, the findings suggest a better starting point: the habitat and the life it supports. What the survey found in Chandigarh’s forests Conducted between 20 and 27 November 2025 by the Chandigarh Department of Forest and Wildlife and the Wildlife Institute of India (WII), the assessment covered Sukhna Wildlife Sanctuary and forest patches beyond its boundaries. Researchers documented 16 mammal species, 132 bird species, 73 butterfly species and 13 species of reptiles and amphibians. They also recorded 43 tree species, 14 shrub species and 22 herb species. The survey detected a leopard and estimated around 603 sambar, a deer species found in the region’s forests. The figures show the variety of life these natural areas continue to shelter. But counting species was only one part of the exercise. The report also looked at the condition of their habitats and recommended restoring native vegetation, protecting grasslands, reviving wetlands and streamside habitats, and controlling invasive species. In Chandigarh, the survey recorded 49 butterfly species in riparian habitats, the areas alongside streams, rivers and other waterbodies. Photograph: (The Tribune) Knowing which animals live in a forest matters. Knowing whether their habitat can continue to support them tells us what needs attention. A forest can have trees and still need help Imagine a woodland full of mature trees. From a distance, it might seem healthy. Look beneath the canopy, though, and there may be very few young trees coming up to replace the older ones. This is the problem of poor natural regeneration, which the Chandigarh survey flagged in native species including khair ( Senegalia catechu ), siris ( Albizia lebbeck ), Lannea coromandelica and Terminalia anogeissiana . Natural regeneration is simply the process of seeds becoming new plants without people planting them. It allows a forest to renew itself across generations. If young trees are missing, some native species could become less common as older trees die. That is why an increase in tree cover cannot, by itself, tell us whether a forest is doing well. The survey also cautioned against large plantations dominated by one species, known as monocultures. A row of identical trees may offer shade, but a healthy habitat needs different kinds of vegetation, from tall trees to shrubs, grasses and ground cover. Each layer has a purpose. Birds need places to nest, butterflies seek nectar, insects live among leaves and grasses, and herbivores depend on suitable plants for food. The report recommends replacing invasive vegetation with native species. Why does that matter? Why native plants can make a difference Native plants occur naturally in a region. Over time, they develop relationships with the insects, birds and animals around them. Some insects feed on particular plants; birds visit their flowers; other animals carry their seeds to new places. Introduced, or exotic, plants come from elsewhere. Many grow successfully in cities, and some offer flowers, fruit or shelter. But they do not always support the same relationships. Certain species can also spread so aggressively that they push out local vegetation. A 2023 Bengaluru study published in Science of the Total Environment helps explain why the distinction matters. Researchers compared how birds and mammals interacted with native and alien trees. They found that taller native trees with larger floral displays supported more bird species than alien trees with comparable displays. There was another interesting difference. Nectar-feeding birds were more likely to visit native flowers in ways that helped pollination. On alien trees, their visits more often involved ‘nectar theft’, where a bird takes nectar without transferring pollen in the way the flower needs to reproduce. This does not mean every introduced tree is harmful. The study recognised that alien trees can provide resources for wildlife in cities where natural vegetation has already been lost. The lesson is to understand what different plants actually offer local wildlife, rather than choosing them only because they grow quickly or look attractive. For Chandigarh, that supports the survey’s recommendation to prioritise native vegetation that belongs to the landscape. Why an open grassland deserves protection A patch of tall, wild grass might look like an empty plot beside a landscaped park. It is easy to imagine someone deciding to plant trees there to ‘improve’ it. But a grassland is already a habitat. Its native grasses feed grazing animals, shelter insects and support species that depend on open spaces. Their roots also help hold soil together and influence how rainwater moves through the ground. Planting trees across an existing grassland can change the conditions that make it useful to those species. The result may look greener to us while offering less to the wildlife that lived there. For cities designing parks, the type of vegetation and its surroundings can matter as much as tree numbers. Photograph: (Chandigarh Help Post) This is why the Chandigarh survey specifically recommended protecting grasslands and restoring native grasses, including Eulaliopsis binata , Arundinella nepalensis and Heteropogon contortus . Across India, open spaces are often treated as land waiting to be developed, tidied up or planted over. Planners first need to ask what habitat is already there. Sometimes, caring for a green space means leaving room for its grasses to grow. Wetlands and riverbanks support different kinds of life The same principle applies to waterbodies and the land around them. In Chandigarh, the survey recorded 49 butterfly species in riparian habitats, the areas alongside streams, rivers and other waterbodies. Woodland habitats, meanwhile, recorded the highest bird diversity. These differences matter. A forest, an open grassland and a stream bank may all be part of the same landscape, yet each offers food and shelter to different species. The report therefore called for wetland restoration and better care of streamside habitats , alongside other measures such as controlling invasive species. Research from the East Kolkata Wetlands shows why protecting such spaces requires attention to more than their size or appearance. A 2024 study in Environmental Research examined changes between 1991 and 2023. It found that the number of wetland patches had risen from 2,689 to 4,532, a sign that the landscape had become more fragmented. Over the same period, the study’s ecosystem health index fell from 0.67 to 0.55. In simple terms, a wetland can still appear on a city map while its connected habitats are broken into smaller pieces and its ecological condition deteriorates. The Kolkata findings do not describe Chandigarh’s wetlands, but they show what cities risk overlooking if they focus only on how much green or blue space remains. The two-day Capacity Building Workshop on Wildlife Survey & Techniques concluded today in Chandigarh! Diverse participants— representatives of civil society organisations, college students, wildlife enthusiasts, media personnel and journalists were sensitized and trained on various wildlife survey and monitoring methods. Thank all the multiple stakeholders for making it impactful. #WildlifeConservation #CitizenScience #WildlifeSurvey #Chandigarh #Sukhna #Chandigarhbirdclub @moefcc @wii_india @GobindsagarBha1 @RuchiBadola2 @gopigv @UDHAYAR230 @Ashik40405287 @Alexjacob11 @NonitaRana04 @RayR5847 — Wildlife Institute of India (@wii_india) November 19, 2025 Chandigarh’s survey also recorded the red-eared slider turtle, an exotic aquatic species, and recommended its removal and management in controlled settings. Such species are sometimes released into waterbodies after being kept as pets and can place additional pressure on native wildlife. Wetlands need care as living habitats, not simply as water-filled spaces. What should other Indian cities measure? There is evidence from Delhi, too, that a park’s value to wildlife depends on more than its tree count. A 2024 study in Ecological Frontiers examined birds across 64 city parks, recording 90 species and 19,131 individual birds. It found that vegetation characteristics and disturbance affected which birds used the parks. Native trees and lower surrounding urbanisation were also linked with greater bird diversity. For cities designing parks, the type of vegetation and its surroundings can matter as much as tree numbers. Chandigarh’s plantation figures offer another lesson. During 2025–26, the administration planted 6,64,133 saplings against a target of 5,76,221. But third-party monitoring in November 2025 and March 2026 found an overall survival rate of around 79%. For 2026–27, the administration lowered its target to 4,19,854 saplings, including those distributed and sold, and said it would pay greater attention to site selection, quality and care after planting. Survival is important. So is asking whether the right species have been planted in the right place, and whether existing habitats are being protected rather than replaced. The Chandigarh survey was conducted over a short period, so its findings are a snapshot rather than proof that the city’s wildlife populations are rising or falling. Longer-term, seasonal monitoring would help show how these habitats and their inhabitants change. But its message is already useful. Before the next plantation drive, city planners can ask a few practical questions: Is this land a forest, grassland or wetland? Which species rely on it? Are young native plants growing back? And what does this place need most? For some spaces, the answer will be trees. For others, it may be restoring a stream bank, protecting a grassland or allowing native shrubs to return. A city’s natural wealth lives in more than its canopy. It is in the butterflies visiting riverbanks, the birds sheltering in woodland, the deer grazing on native grasses and the many smaller creatures that depend on them. Making room for all these habitats is how a city makes room for wildlife. items.title: 2 Friends Saw Value in the Straw That Farmers Burn. Today, Their Business Makes Rs 8 Crore in Sales
items.blurb: Every year, once the paddy harvest is over, farmers across Haryana face a familiar problem. Their fields are covered with leftover straw, and they need to clear the land before planting the next crop. For many, burning this stubble is the quickest solution. But the smoke that rises from these fields adds to North India’s already severe air pollution. Now imagine if that same straw could earn money, create jobs and even help power industries. That’s exactly what two women from Haryana and neighbouring Rajasthan set out to do. Sanjana, a graduate from Ghoranwali village in Haryana’s Sirsa district, and her friend Sonika, from Bhadra in Rajasthan, saw a business opportunity in something farmers struggled to get rid of. They decided to collect leftover paddy straw , locally called parali , and turn it into biofuel pellets that power plants could use as an alternative fuel. In 2024, they started SSAR Biomass Green Private Limited with an investment of approximately Rs 2.5 crore. Today, the venture reports an annual turnover of Rs 7–8 crore and employs over 20 people. From a pollution problem to a business idea For Sonika, the idea began with a sight she had witnessed repeatedly after the paddy harvest: thick smoke spreading across the sky as farmers burned crop residue. Concerned about the environmental and public health consequences, she began thinking about how this agricultural waste could be put to better use. Rather than treating stubble burning as a problem with no easy solution, she and Sanjana started exploring ways to convert the residue into a commercially useful product. At their manufacturing unit in Ghoranwali, Haryana, machinery processes leftover paddy straw into compact biofuel pellets, giving agricultural waste a productive use. Photograph: ( Peddler media ) The idea was to address two needs together: give farmers a productive use for their leftover crop residue while creating an alternative fuel that industries could use. Government policies and initiatives promoting stubble management also helped create an opportunity for the venture to take shape. Building a factory around farm waste In 2024, Sanjana and Sonika set up their manufacturing unit in Ghoranwali with an investment of approximately Rs 2.5 crore under the Agriculture Infrastructure Fund (AIF) scheme. The factory follows a process that begins in the fields. The women source paddy straw through baler operators in Sirsa and surrounding areas. These operators collect and compress the loose residue, making it easier to transport and store. The stubble is then brought to their factory, where machinery processes it into compact biofuel pellets. These pellets can be supplied to power plants as an alternative fuel. By sourcing paddy straw from farmers and baler operators across the region, the founders are creating a market for crop residue. Photograph: (AI generated using reference) The scale of the operation is considerable. The unit uses approximately 1 lakh to 1.5 lakh quintals of paddy stubble every year. Since the raw material is available mainly during the harvesting season, the founders also have to plan for the months ahead. They collect and store the residue after harvest, ensuring that the factory has enough raw material to continue production throughout the year. This seasonal sourcing and year-round production model allows them to keep the business running beyond the harvesting window. From discarded straw to a growing rural enterprise The venture's impact extends beyond the pellets it produces. By creating a market for paddy straw, SSAR Biomass Green Private Limited also generates business opportunities for local baler operators and others involved in collecting and transporting the residue. The factory itself provides employment to more than 20 people, bringing work opportunities closer to home for residents in and around the village. From an initial investment of approximately Rs 2.5 crore, Sanjana and Sonika have built an enterprise reporting an annual turnover of Rs 7–8 crore. What began as an effort to address stubble burning has grown into a rural enterprise that employs over 20 people and reports an annual turnover of Rs 8 crore. Photograph: ( Peddler Media ) For the two founders, the next harvest season will bring another opportunity to source more stubble, keep production going and expand their business. Their work has given farmers in the region another possible route for managing crop residue, while creating a market for material that would otherwise have little economic value. In Ghoranwali, the paddy harvest no longer marks just the end of a farming cycle. For Sanjana and Sonika, it also marks the beginning of another season of business, one built around putting farm waste to productive use. items.title: The Lights We Leave On Could Be Taking Away the Darkness Kerala’s Forests Need. Here’s How to Help
items.blurb: A road outside a forest stays lit after sunset. So does a nearby place of worship or a cluster of shops where people gather. Those lights help people go about their lives. But their glow can travel beyond the places they are meant to illuminate. For wildlife living in Kerala’s Western Ghats, that raises an important question: how much of the night inside protected forests is still naturally dark? A team of four researchers has begun answering it. Their study, published in Biological Conservation in October 2026, mapped artificial light in and around 21 protected areas in Kerala and examined the roads, buildings and other human activities associated with it. Their findings reveal a conservation concern that is easy to overlook: even where forests have protected boundaries, light from surrounding areas can still reach them. What's causing the forests to light up? Using satellite data from 2024, researchers S. Haripriya, M.S. Arjun, S. Gopakumar and Vijayan Divya measured night-time light across national parks and wildlife sanctuaries. They then compared those measurements with maps showing nearby roads, places of worship, buildings and centres of human activity. The difference between forests was striking. Periyar Tiger Reserve's western division recorded the highest average and peak levels of satellite-measured light among the 21 areas, with a mean radiance of 0.369 and a maximum of 24.0. Kerala's protected areas include tropical evergreen forests, semi-evergreen forests, shola-grassland ecosystems and riverine habitats. Photograph: (Tiger Safari Tours India) Within protected areas, the strongest statistical link was with the density of places of worship. In the surrounding landscape, road networks and places where people gather or work were more important predictors. That distinction matters. Light affecting a forest may be associated with several kinds of human activity, and managing it requires knowing where to look. But light does not always arrive as a visible beam. It can scatter through the atmosphere and brighten the night sky over places some distance away. Researchers call this skyglow . The team examined areas extending up to 30 km beyond forest boundaries. Their modelling suggested that the wider surrounding landscape, particularly the 10–30 km zone, could contribute substantially to skyglow. This means lighting decisions made several kilometres away may influence how dark a protected forest remains at night. Why does darkness matter to wildlife? The Western Ghats are home to many species found nowhere else, including animals active after dark. Natural cycles of light and darkness help wildlife navigate, find food and follow daily rhythms. Research elsewhere has shown that artificial lighting can alter animal behaviour. However, the Kerala study did not directly observe animals or measure how they were affected. That distinction is important. The researchers have identified where artificial light is present and which features of the surrounding landscape are associated with it. Understanding what those light levels mean for different species will require further research. Lead author S. Haripriya has also expressed an interest in investigating these ecological effects in future. Could simple lighting changes help protect these forests? For forest departments and local authorities, the study offers something immediately useful: a way to identify areas where lighting deserves closer attention. A brightly lit road near a forest edge could be assessed for lamps that shine upwards or sideways. Places of worship and tourism facilities could review whether lights need to remain on at full strength throughout the night. Shielded fixtures, lower-intensity lighting and switching off unnecessary lights during periods of low activity are among the options worth considering, while keeping public safety in mind. Periyar Tiger Reserve's western division recorded the highest average and peak levels of satellite-measured light among the 21 areas, with a mean radiance of 0.369 and a maximum of 24.0. Photograph: (Deccan Herald) These are possible next steps rather than changes already implemented because of the study. The findings could, however, help forest officials, local communities and those responsible for public lighting decide where action would be most useful. For years, protecting forests has meant paying attention to what happens within their boundaries. This research offers a reason to look beyond those boundaries, too. And sometimes, protecting a forest's natural environment may begin with something as simple as reconsidering where, when and how we use light. items.title: Same City, Different Sources of Pollution: What Ahmedabad’s Air Data Reveals
items.blurb: A patch of dust near a busy road, smoke rising from an industrial chimney, and waste burning in an open space may all contribute to a city's air pollution. But the sources responsible for poor air quality are not necessarily the same across neighbourhoods. This means that a measure addressing pollution in one part of a city may not be equally effective elsewhere. Understanding what contributes to poor air quality at specific locations is therefore an important part of planning cleaner cities . Ahmedabad is attempting to address this challenge by looking beyond citywide air-quality readings and examining pollution at specific locations. The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC), in collaboration with IIT Kanpur, has identified 10 locations across the city for a real-time air-quality monitoring initiative called SMART-VAYU. Reported by The Times of India (TOI) on September 30, 2026, the project aims to identify local pollution hotspots, trace the sources of emissions and generate data that can help civic authorities plan targeted interventions. Initial monitoring exercises at two locations — Sabarmati Riverfront Sports Complex and Narendra Modi Stadium — have already revealed how pollution sources can differ within the same city. One city, two different pollution profiles The initial findings from Ahmedabad offer an interesting look at how the sources contributing to air pollution can vary from one location to another. In its October 17, 2026 report, TOI detailed the findings from air-quality sampling at the Sabarmati Riverfront Sports Complex and Narendra Modi Stadium. Sampling at the riverfront was conducted between May 4 and May 24, while monitoring at Narendra Modi Stadium took place between June 25 and August 8. At the Sabarmati Riverfront, dust accounted for 36% of the estimated source contribution, compared with 23% at Narendra Modi Stadium. Coal combustion contributed 24% at the riverfront, while its estimated contribution at the stadium was just 1%. The pattern was different at Motera. The combined category of marine emissions and refuse burning accounted for 38% of the estimated pollution sources at Narendra Modi Stadium, compared with 16% at the riverfront. Power plant-related sources contributed another 20% at the stadium. The analysis also examined different types of organic aerosols. Traffic-related organic aerosols contributed 18% at Narendra Modi Stadium and 13% at the riverfront. Solid-fuel combustion-related organic aerosols accounted for 16% at the stadium and 5% at the riverfront. These findings highlight an important aspect of urban air pollution: even within one city, different locations can have different pollution profiles . Understanding these differences can help authorities identify which sources need attention in specific areas, rather than approaching air pollution as a uniform problem across the city. Why Ahmedabad is looking beyond citywide AQI readings Identifying the sources behind air pollution is not always straightforward. Citywide air-quality readings provide information about pollution levels, but understanding what is contributing to poor air quality in a particular neighbourhood requires more detailed monitoring. This is the gap that SMART-VAYU aims to address. The initiative stands for Sensing and Monitoring for Air Quality using Real-time Technology – Vision-based Ahmedabad air analysis for Urban Management. The project involves three broad components: mapping existing pollution sources, establishing a hyperlocal monitoring network and developing a decision-support system for urban air-quality management. For civic authorities, this distinction could help connect monitoring with specific pollution-control measures. Photograph: (Ahmedabad Mirror) For this, AMC and IIT Kanpur finalised 10 monitoring locations across Ahmedabad. These include Sabarmati Riverfront Sports Complex, Narendra Modi Stadium, Gujarat Police Academy at Karai, Sanskardham, Veer Savarkar Sports Complex, Pirana AMC community service centre, Rakhial AMC health office, Vatva GIDC's Chandrakala complex, Bopal urban health centre and Thaltej AMC ward office. The selection considered meteorological conditions, particulate matter readings, annual wind patterns, satellite-based aerosol optical depth and estimated PM2.5 concentrations. Practical requirements such as electricity, security, accessibility and airflow were also taken into account. The plan is to deploy five locations with mobile laboratory sampling alongside sensors, while the remaining five will have fixed sensors. The wider project envisages eventually expanding the network to around 400 sensors across Ahmedabad. How the monitoring network will identify pollution sources Unlike conventional monitoring systems that primarily provide broader air-quality readings, these sensors will continuously measure pollutants such as PM2.5, PM10, nitrogen oxides, carbon monoxide, ozone and sulphur dioxide. They will also record meteorological parameters, including temperature and humidity. The Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC), in collaboration with IIT Kanpur, has identified 10 locations across the city for a real-time air-quality monitoring. Photograph: (Hindustan Times) An important component is the mobile Real-Time Source Apportionment Laboratory (RTSA), which will help examine the contribution of different pollution sources. Source apportionment is the process of estimating how much different sources contribute to the pollutants present in the air. These could include vehicular emissions, industrial activity, road dust, construction and waste burning. By examining these contributions, the initiative aims to generate pollution hotspot maps, forecasts and alerts that can help authorities identify locations requiring attention. From identifying pollution to planning targeted action Ahmedabad already has an air-quality monitoring network under the Centre's System of Air Quality and Weather Forecasting and Research (SAFAR) programme. Its monitoring stations provide city-level air-quality information and forecasts. SMART-VAYU seeks to add another layer of information by examining pollution sources at specific locations. For civic authorities, this distinction could help connect monitoring with specific pollution-control measures. For instance, identifying road dust as a major contributor could inform dust-control and road-cleaning measures. Similarly, evidence of industrial emissions or waste burning could help direct inspections and enforcement. The effectiveness of the initiative will depend on how consistently the monitoring network operates, whether its findings translate into enforceable measures and how improvements in air quality are tracked over time. Ultimately, Ahmedabad's initiative highlights why tackling urban air pollution requires more than understanding how polluted a city is. It also requires knowing what is polluting different parts of it. Because when pollution sources vary from one neighbourhood to another, the solutions must account for those differences too. items.title: TRYING HARD TO LOSE WEIGHT?BUT IS YOUR BODY PUSHING BACK?
items.blurb: “Just eat less.” “Work harder.” “Have some willpower.” We hear it all the time. But if weight loss were that simple, why can keeping it off feel even harder? Because sometimes, your own biology pushes back. After you lose weight, your body can respond with stronger hunger signals and lower energy use. These biological adaptations can favour weight regain. Does that mean weight always comes back? No. It means long-term medical support may need more than a short burst of willpower. And struggling doesn’t mean someone is lazy or lacks discipline. Weight is shaped by biology, behaviour and environment. If you keep struggling, continue with practical nutrition, movement, strength and sleep habits. And if weight repeatedly returns, or the plan feels impossible to sustain, speak to a qualified doctor about long-term weight management and the biological or practical barriers involved. Getting medical support is not failure. Talk to a qualified doctor about your weight management. items.title: Empty Corners at Home? These 10 Tall Indoor Plants Can Fill Them With Greenery
items.blurb: Festive decorations bring colour and warmth to a home, but a little greenery can make the space feel even more inviting. If you want to give your living room, entrance, or balcony a fresh look this festive season, tall indoor plants are a lovely way to do it. They add height, fill empty corners, and bring a natural charm to your decorations. Pair them with earthen pots, warm fairy lights, or a few diyas , and these plants can become part of your festive decor. Here are 10 tall houseplants worth considering. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Lazy Gardener (@lazygardener.in) 1. Rubber Plant With its broad, glossy leaves and upright growth, the rubber plant makes a striking addition to any room. Its deep green foliage looks particularly beautiful against light-coloured walls. It prefers bright, indirect light and watering when the top layer of soil dries out. The rubber plant makes a striking addition to any room. Photograph: (Leaf Envy) 2. Bird of Paradise Known for its large, banana-like leaves, the bird of paradise brings a tropical feel indoors. Given enough light and space, it can grow quite tall. Place it near a bright window and water when the soil begins to dry. Known for its large, banana-like leaves, the bird of paradise brings a tropical feel indoors. Photograph: (Plant Drop) 3. Money Tree The money tree is loved for its distinctive braided trunk and clusters of green leaves. Usually associated with prosperity and good fortune, it makes a fitting addition to festive homes. It grows well in bright, indirect light and prefers well-draining soil. The money tree is loved for its distinctive braided trunk and clusters of green leaves. Photograph: (Patch Plants) 4. Areca Palm Its arching, feathery fronds give the areca palm a soft, tropical appearance. It works particularly well in living rooms and near entrances where it has room to spread. Keep it in bright, indirect light and maintain lightly moist soil. Its arching, feathery fronds give the areca palm a soft, tropical appearance. Photograph: (Amazon.in) 5. Monstera The monstera stands out for its large, naturally split leaves. Its dramatic foliage adds character without requiring complicated decoration. It prefers bright, indirect light and moderate watering . Give it a moss pole or support as it grows. The monstera stands out for its large, naturally split leaves. Photograph: (unlimitedgreens) 6. Fiddle Leaf Fig With its oversized, violin-shaped leaves, the fiddle leaf fig makes a beautiful statement plant. It looks especially elegant in a simple ceramic planter. Place it in a bright spot with indirect sunlight and avoid moving it around frequently. With its oversized, violin-shaped leaves, the fiddle-leaf fig makes a beautiful statement plant. Photograph: (Mason Home) 7. Dracaena Dracaena varieties are known for their upright growth and attractive foliage. Some have slender leaves with colourful edges, making them a good choice for narrow corners. They prefer indirect light and need watering only when the soil starts drying out. Dracaena varieties are known for their upright growth and attractive foliage. Photograph: (Thursd) 8. Yucca The yucca’s woody stem and pointed leaves give it a distinctive, sculptural appearance. It is a good option for those who prefer plants that need less frequent watering. Keep it near a sunny window and allow the soil to dry between waterings. The yucca’s woody stem and pointed leaves give it a distinctive, sculptural appearance. Photograph: (Fourwalls) 9. Elephant Ear As the name suggests, elephant ear plants have enormous, heart-shaped leaves that instantly catch the eye. Their lush foliage brings a tropical touch to indoor spaces. They prefer bright, indirect light, humidity, and consistently moist, well-draining soil. As the name suggests, elephant ear plants have enormous, heart-shaped leaves that instantly catch the eye. Photograph: (Bloomica) 10. Croton If your festive decor needs a burst of colour, the croton is a wonderful choice. Its leaves feature captivating shades of green, yellow, orange, and red. It needs plenty of bright light to maintain its vibrant colours and should be watered when the topsoil begins to dry. If your festive decor needs a burst of colour, the croton is a wonderful choice. Photograph: (Nista) Whether you prefer the deep green leaves of a rubber plant or the colourful foliage of a Croton, these houseplants can give your home a festive makeover that lasts well beyond the celebrations. Choose plants according to the light and space available, dress up their pots, and let the greenery do the rest.

items.title: Millions Had His Painting. Few Knew His Name!
items.blurb: Copy: For over five decades, his artwork found a place in millions of Indian homes, becoming a familiar sight across generations. Artist S.M. Srinivasan, who passed away at 86, was known for his paintings of deities, especially his two iconic depictions of Lord Venkateswara, which became widely recognised through calendars, posters and framed prints. Born in Kovilpatti, Tamil Nadu, Srinivasan studied up to Class 10 before learning the art of painting under renowned artist Kondaiah Raju. In 1970, he got a rare opportunity to observe and paint the idol at the Tirumala temple. He created two versions, one with elaborate ornaments and another without them. Approved by the Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanams (TTD), his paintings were reproduced as calendars, posters and framed prints. Soon, his artwork became a familiar sight on calendars across India, finding its way into homes, shops and everyday spaces. For generations, these familiar images became part of India’s visual and cultural landscape. While many may not have known the artist behind them, his work remained a part of their everyday lives. #Srinivasan #SMSrinivasan #TirupatiBalaji #IndianArt [S.M. items.title: ‘I Thought I Was Bad at Art’: How a Museum Is Changing the Way Children See Their Creativity
items.blurb: “I felt that there were opportunities to draw and participate in school activities, but there were fewer chances for children to showcase their work to a wider audience.” For 18-year-old Sahil Santosh Kundojwar, art was something he enjoyed creating but mostly shared with teachers, friends, and family. He had opportunities to draw at school, but finding an audience beyond his immediate circle was not easy. That changed in July 2024, when a teacher at The Aditya Birla Public School in Awarpur, Maharashtra, introduced him to the Children’s Art Museum of India (CAMI). He submitted a drawing of Ganpati Bappa for a theme called ‘My Superhero’. It won a prize, giving him the encouragement to share more of his work. “I didn’t expect to win a prize, so receiving recognition for my Ganpati artwork was a very special and motivating experience for me,” he says. His story reflects the idea behind CAMI, a digital museum that gives children a dedicated space to display their artwork. Founded in January 2022 by cousins Krish Nawal and Manya Roongta, the platform has grown to more than 3 lakh registered members. Its collection includes over 20,000 artworks, and the website has received more than a million visitors from over 200 towns and cities. The idea began with a question the siblings found themselves asking during COVID-19. Children were creating art at home, but where could they go to have it seen, appreciated, and preserved? A museum of their own During the pandemic, the siblings were spending more time at home and creating art themselves. They noticed that children around them were doing the same, but much of this work stayed in school notebooks, folders, or at home, with few opportunities to reach a wider audience. Founded in January 2022 by cousins Krish Nawal and Manya Roongta, CAMI has grown to more than 3 lakh registered members. They felt that children’s artwork should not be limited to occasional displays at school exhibitions or relegated to a corner of a museum primarily meant for adults. They wanted to build a space where young artists would be at the centre. Krish recalls the question that set the idea in motion. “Why wasn’t there a space where a child could say, ‘This is my artwork, and it belongs in a museum’?” Krish, now 16 and a Class 11 student at The Shri Ram School in Gurugram, and Manya, 19, who is pursuing a bachelor’s degree in the United States, began working on the idea together. For the 16-year-old, the aim was to change how children viewed their own creations. “I wanted to create a space where children could see their artwork displayed, feel that it mattered, and know that it deserved to be seen,” he says. Manya wanted the experience to feel different from uploading an image online. “We did not want to create just another website where children could upload pictures. We wanted the artwork to have a context and a sense of recognition,” she tells The Better India . Turning that idea into a functioning museum meant learning almost everything from scratch. The siblings began with an Excel spreadsheet, mapping out how children would submit their work and how the museum would organise and display it. They experimented with WordPress and Wix to build early versions of the website and emailed schools and children to gauge interest. There was no established organisation or technical team behind them. They learnt about website development, communication, curation, and outreach as they went along, with their parents helping them through the early stages. “The first step was deciding that we were going to build it rather than keep talking about it,” Krish says. The website went live in January 2022. Its first version was uncomplicated, allowing children to submit artwork and have it displayed in an online collection. The first submission was a picture of a peacock sent in by a young child. Because the website did not yet require all the details it collects today, the founders knew very little about the artist. They have even tried to trace her since. Krish remembers the submission for what it represented. “There was just a child who had created something and wanted a place to share it,” he says. Where young artists find recognition As children began finding the platform, CAMI grew beyond its original digital collection. The founders started introducing programmes that would give young artists regular reasons to create and share their work. One such initiative is the monthly ArtFest. Each edition revolves around a theme or creative prompt, which children can interpret in their own way before submitting their artwork. Selected entries are showcased as part of the programme. For Krish, the aim was to change how children viewed their own creations. The idea is to encourage participation rather than make creativity depend on winning a competition. Manya says the team wanted children to have opportunities to return to the platform and keep experimenting. “We realised that children should not have to wait for one opportunity to submit their artwork. We wanted our initiative to give them regular reasons to create, participate, and explore,” she says. CAMI also works with schools through dedicated galleries , ArtFests, and other creative initiatives. These programmes allow students to display their work beyond the classroom. Its collaborations include Sarvodaya schools in Delhi, the Aditya Birla Group, and Bagiya Foundation. Children aged three to 18 can submit their artwork through the website. Each entry goes through a verification process to ensure it is appropriate for children. Art teachers, curators, and members of the core team review submissions, generally within 24 to 48 hours. The team considers originality, effort, and creative expression rather than expecting professional-level technique. Accepted artwork becomes part of the digital collection or may be considered for an ArtFest, exhibition, or school gallery. Children also receive a CAMI certificate. “We are not looking for technical perfection. A child’s artwork does not need to look professionally executed to have value,” explains the teen founder. The museum has also developed a learning section with resources on creating, appreciating, and understanding different art forms. These include traditional and indigenous Indian styles such as Warli, Madhubani, and Pattachitra. Children and visitors can also engage with CAMI through its YouTube channel and Spotify podcast. In 2023, the founders took the museum into another digital environment by launching a virtual museum on Roblox. With more than 120 million daily active users globally, the platform offered a way to reach children in a space where they already play, create, and connect. The virtual museum allows players to walk through galleries and view artwork made by children. It has received over 2,70,600 visits, extending the reach of the collection beyond the conventional website. What recognition can mean to a young artist? For the founders, the value of the initiative is not measured only through membership figures or the number of artworks in its collection. Some of the most meaningful moments have come through the responses they receive from children. Manya remembers an Instagram message from a girl who was around 12. After seeing her painting displayed in the museum, the child wrote, “I used to think I wasn’t good at art, but when you displayed my painting in the museum, I began to feel that maybe I was,” she recalls. The founders started introducing programmes that would give young artists regular reasons to create and share their work. The message stayed with the co-founder because it showed how being taken seriously could change a child’s perception of their own ability. “She was not suddenly a professional artist, and nothing about her artistic ability had changed overnight. What changed was that someone had taken her work seriously enough to give it a place,” she says. Manya has also seen how children’s creative expression changes as they continue making and sharing art. Some begin with familiar drawings of two mountains and the sun, but gradually experiment with portraits, posters, different compositions, and styles such as cubism and modern art. “For me, that progression is not really about becoming a ‘better’ artist in a technical sense. It is about becoming more confident in having an idea of their own and being willing to experiment with it,” she says. Seventeen-year-old Kritika from Delhi has experienced some of that encouragement herself. Before joining CAMI in September this year, she mostly shared her artwork with family or during school art classes. She wanted to see her work displayed alongside that of other children and hoped for feedback that would help her take herself seriously as an artist. Her first submission, titled ‘Fish Illusion’, was accepted for the online gallery. Seeing it published encouraged her to begin working on another project. “When I first submitted my artwork on the website, I hoped that my work would be accepted and displayed on a real platform. I wanted to see how it looked alongside other children’s art and hoped to get some encouragement or feedback that would make me feel like a real artist,” she says. Her parents’ response to the painting also stayed with her. They complimented her use of colours and told her that the artwork had brought a smile to their faces. “That made me realise that my art has the power to make people happy,” she adds. Having her work displayed on the platform has made her more comfortable sharing it with others. “Now, I feel incredibly proud to show people my work and confidently call myself an artist,” she says. Sahil, too, explains that the recognition he received through CAMI made him more confident about putting his work forward. Appreciation from teachers and classmates after winning the Monthly Best Prize encouraged him to participate in more activities. He has one piece of advice for young artists. “I would tell them not to be afraid or shy about showing their work. If you are proud of what you have created, you should share it with others because your creativity is special and unique . Don’t worry about whether everyone will like it,” he says. Building a community across India As the initiative developed its programmes, its reach began extending beyond the founders’ immediate circles. What started with children from familiar schools and communities now includes participants from major cities as well as smaller towns and villages. CAMI also works with schools through dedicated galleries, ArtFests, and other creative initiatives. The founders cite participation from places such as Vaniyambadi, Rampurhat, Guntur, Nainital, Khammam, Ranaghat, Patna, Bareilly, Nagpur, Coimbatore, Kanhagad, Prayagraj, Kota, and Puducherry. The platform has also reached villages in Uttarakhand and smaller communities in West Bengal and Odisha. Manya says the geographical spread has been one of the most surprising aspects of the journey. A digital museum, she explains, allows a child from a smaller town to participate in the same collection as someone living in a major city. The first major sign that CAMI was gaining momentum came by June 2022, when the team began receiving artwork submissions every day. Its first school collaboration showed the founders that they could reach groups of children through educators, rather than relying only on individual submissions. The Roblox museum, launched the following year, opened another route to young audiences. The initiative now has a core team of five members, supported by more than 20 volunteers and over 500 young brand ambassadors. It continues to operate as a bootstrapped initiative, with the founders relying on their own resources and family support rather than institutional venture funding. Their roles have changed as the museum has grown. Krish, who initially handled everything from the website and social media to school outreach and submissions, now focuses more on its development, operations, and future direction. Manya’s responsibilities centre on ideation, marketing, outreach, and programme development. Building the initiative while studying has also taught them to manage their time and share responsibilities. Krish works on the initiative after school and during weekends, while prioritising academics during examinations. As the team has expanded, he has learnt to delegate rather than remain involved in every task. “I often say that school taught me how to learn, but CAMI taught me how to turn ideas into something real,” he says. The siblings are now looking at ways to create more opportunities for young artists. These include exhibitions, local art initiatives led by ambassadors and avenues through which children can have their artwork commissioned. The co-founder sees this as a natural next step for a platform built around recognising young people’s creativity. Children aged three to 18 can submit their artwork through the website. “If we tell children that their creative work has value, we should also think about how we can create real opportunities around that value,” he says. From an Excel spreadsheet and a simple website to a community of more than 3 lakh registered members, CAMI has grown considerably since 2022. At its core, it continues to champion the idea that children’s creativity deserves to be taken seriously , giving young artists the encouragement and recognition to keep creating. All pictures courtesy CAMI.

items.title: Kemi and Andy put another nail in the coffin of his consensus politics | John Crace
items.blurb:
The Tory leader is hardwired for conflict. It was futile for the PM to demand an end to her patronising tone

Well, that didn’t take long. When Andy Burnham first arrived in No 10, he said he was determined to do things differently. He wanted a new, consensual politics where he would work with other parties to put the country back together. Safe to say, that dream is already dead in the water. At least when it comes to his exchanges with Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions.

Andy might go through the motions of promising Ed Davey and various backbenchers a veneer of cross-party support that may or may not become reality – even Andy doesn’t have a clue which is which – but when it comes to Kemi, it’s now just a bloodless slanging match. items.title: Annoying Trump and dodging Flock: inside MapQuest’s contrarian comeback

I am among the legion of former PC desk occupants with warm memories of MapQuest, the Y2K-era travel website that kept millennial drivers on course with sheaves of printed-out directions – a quantum leap over the ungainly glovebox map. But I assumed it had long since gone the way of AIM and Skype, its manual turn-by-turn guidance made obsolete by big tech.

Proof of life came in January 2025, when Donald Trump issued an executive order renaming the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America – a change Apple Maps and Google Maps promptly adopted, while MapQuest … did nothing. Not only had it never signed off, MapQuest was reinventing itself as a plucky oppositional hero, the app most likely to uphold your geographical beliefs.

Milburn’s absurdly ambitious report offers blueprint for fixing everything and everyone
items.blurb:
He lays out sweeping aims and finer details for how to fix the Neets crisis – and is obsessive about welfare

  • Neet ideas: what’s in Milburn’s report?

It is not clear if too many people were expecting Everything Everywhere All at Once, but that is what Alan Milburn has delivered. From a Welfare State to a Working State is almost absurdly ambitious. The terms of reference said something about the drivers of youth labour markets. We got a blueprint for how to fix everything and everyone.

What Keir Starmer, who commissioned it, had in mind, we’ll never know, but Milburn has taken up with gusto Andy Burnham’s general invocation to think boldly and rewire the state. Yes, it’s about training and jobs, but it’s also about pulling apart the NHS, giving schools and colleges an MOT, and once again, blowing up old-fashioned social security.

The final week of Cop31 is in full swing, with just four days left to set a broad range of climate commitments into concrete action. I am on the ground at this year’s UN annual climate summit, where thousands of world leaders, businesses, nonprofits and scientists have converged in Antalya, Turkey, and there’s a lot left to do as the clock ticks down.

“Nearly 200 countries are working through 165 mandates,” executive secretary Simon Stiell told reporters at the midpoint on Saturday, pushing for a swift move to the hardest issues and championing compromise. “Each country has a view,” he said. “Every country has a voice.”

items.title: Menopause symptoms aren’t always taken seriously. These female lawmakers plan to change that
items.blurb:
From Utah to Louisiana, US states are making menopause care more affordable and accessible for midlife women

Melissa Shusterman was desperate for help with her menopausal symptoms: body aches, lethargy and brain fog, which she described as feeling “not myself”. The Pennsylvania state representative saw a gynecologist, a physical therapist, a chiropractor and a urologist. One doctor gave her lubricant, even though she’d already explained to him that sex was not the problem. (“Have you seen my husband?” she quipped.)

“I am more than lubrication,” Shusterman said. “I am a dynamic, smart, hardworking woman who wants to continue to feel good, so I can join my contemporaries, get back to work, and change things.”
